Summary and premise
No single study has been found that simultaneously and systematically combines zeolite, biochar, lime, elemental sulfur (or sulfate sources), and fungal mycelium into one process for “severe” oil‑contaminated soil remediation. This is not because the idea is unripe, but because the physicochemical nature of petroleum hydrocarbons (highly hydrophobic TPHs, PAHs, and mixed organosulfur/nitrogen compounds), the strong interactions among these amendments (especially lime–sulfur), and the niche ecological requirements of fungal systems create layered constraints that make such co‑amendment uncommon in current literature and field practice. Adjacent lines of evidence do, however, show each component’s role, composite benefits, and the limitations that must be overcome to integrate them, which explains the current state of the art and points to feasible pathways forward. <cite id="e3be1b9e-3">Petroleum hydrocarbon mixtures consist of alkanes, aromatics, and trace sulfur/nitrogenous compounds, and their concentrations are highest near oil and gas infrastructure</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-0">Biochar, zeolite, and clay are common adsorbents in soil pollution remediation</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Mycoremediation is promising for aliphatic hydrocarbons but limited by knowledge gaps and scale-up challenges</cite> <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Heavy hydrocarbons often persist for years to decades; biodegradation depends on redox and environmental conditions, and physical effects like hydrophobicity and oil crusts limit oxygen diffusion</cite>.

What the literature actually does today
- Biochar as a central enabler: Across oil‑contaminated soils, biochar consistently improves hydrocarbon removal by adsorbing/immobilizing pollutants, supplying redox hotspots, improving water retention, and supplying mineral nutrients (N, P, K) and functional groups that stimulate microbial communities and TPH biodegradation. <cite id="b5c55970-1">Biochar reduces TPH mobility via sorption and nutrient amendment; nitrogen increased 23–16%, phosphorus by 10–5%, and potassium by 5–3% under 10–15% contamination compared with no biochar</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-2">Biochar amendments significantly increased bacterial populations (R2 ≈ 0.50) and degradation efficiency versus nutrients alone</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-3">Under optimized preparation, biochar’s adsorption capacity can surpass zeolite/clay via high surface area and diverse mechanisms</cite> <cite id="e3be1b9e-3">Biochar increased total petroleum hydrocarbon removal to over 67% in 60 days in one study, with enrichment of petroleum‑degrading bacteria</cite>.
- Zeolite and composites: Natural zeolites immobilize metals via ion exchange and physical adsorption, and biochar–zeolite composites can synergistically reduce heavy metal bioavailability while improving nutrient conditions and soil function. <cite id="b5c55970-0">Zeolite relies on ion exchange and physical adsorption and is especially effective for cations, whereas biochar offers more diverse adsorption mechanisms</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-3">A biochar–zeolite composite reduced Cd bioavailability by 59.7–68.5% and improved mechanical stability for soil application</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-4">Biochar plus zeolite together can reduce the concentration and mobility of active Cd by complementary mechanisms (stable carbon matrix vs. ion exchange/adsorption)</cite>.
- Fungi/mycelium: Filamentous fungi and white‑rot species degrade hydrocarbons via extracellular oxidative enzymes, with mycelia penetrating oil to increase surface area and facilitate bacterial attack; however, field scale‑up is limited by knowledge gaps, nutrient availability, humidity, oxygen diffusion, and interactions with indigenous microbiota. <cite id="d26ca954-0">Fungal mycelium is a bioremediation strategy; fungi secrete extracellular enzymes, tolerate stress, and fungi–bacteria consortia synergistically degrade recalcitrant pollutants</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-1">White‑rot fungi (e.g., Polyporus, Phanerochaete) and keratinolytic fungi have been used to remove aliphatic hydrocarbons and crude oil mixtures</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Few bench‑scale mycoremediation experiences exist; effectiveness hinges on bioavailability, fungal selection, bulking agents, nutrient status, and environmental factors such as humidity, oxygen, and temperature</cite>.
- Lime/sulfur and redox control: Soil amendments are used to adjust pH and redox to increase hydrocarbon bioavailability and steer microbial metabolism (e.g., to sulfidogenic conditions), but hydrophobicity and sorption to organic matter/Fe/Al oxides remain major bottlenecks; biodegradation kinetics are slow and highly context‑dependent. <cite id="344bd8fa-0">Bioremediation depends on hydrocarbon bioavailability, which can be enhanced via microbial surface modification, solubilization, and desorption</cite> <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Biodegradation of heavy hydrocarbons is strongly redox‑dependent and can persist for years; soil hydrophobicity and oil crusts reduce oxygen diffusion</cite>.
- Integration precedents: Multi‑component stacks are already practiced. Plants–microbes–biochar systems leverage rhizosphere and mycorrhizal interactions to enhance hydrocarbon degradation, and combined plant–microbe remediation often still requires suitable soil amendments. <cite id="e3be1b9e-2">Rhizoremediation and mycorrhizosphere development enhance bacterial use of carbon sources and degradation of petroleum pollution; practical applications often still require soil amendments like biochar</cite> <cite id="e3be1b9e-0">Biochar obtained from rice straw remediated crude oil‑contaminated soil efficiently; grasses with extensive root systems and nutrient supplementation improved remediation</cite>.

Why a single study combining all five components is rare
1) Physicochemical constraints of oil mixtures and nutrient/cation competition
- Petroleum hydrocarbons are highly hydrophobic and tend to sorb to organic matter and Fe/Al oxides; raising pH with lime and adding carbonaceous materials (biochar) changes sorption and desorption equilibria, while sulfur amendments can create sulfide via Fe–S, altering metal bioavailability and potentially interfering with fungal enzymatic systems. These interactions are complex and sensitive; without careful sequencing and dosing, amendments can reduce microbial access or create toxic conditions. <cite id="b5c55970-0">Biochar provides diverse adsorption mechanisms and can simultaneously address multiple contaminants, outperforming ion‑exchange‑dominated zeolite for a broad range of pollutants</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-4">Combined biochar–zeolite amendments can improve immobilization of metals by complementary mechanisms</cite> <cite id="344bd8fa-0">Bioavailability—enhanced via desorption and solubilization—is a prerequisite for bioremediation</cite>.
- Lime and sulfur are strong operators on pH and redox. Lime elevates pH, often increasing PAH sorption to minerals and reducing their aqueous bioavailability; sulfur/oxyferric sulfur can drive sequential acidification and sulfide formation that mobilizes metals. Getting the sequence and dosage “right” to avoid transient toxicity and to maintain adequate carbon/nutrient availability for fungal mycelium is nontrivial. <cite id="b5c55970-0">Zeolite’s ion‑exchange capacity is strong for cations, but mechanisms differ from biochar and clay; mechanisms interact with soil chemistry</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-1">Biochar’s nutrient supplementation (N, P, K) can directly support microbial growth</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Fungal degradation effectiveness depends on soil nutrients and interactions with indigenous microbiota</cite>.
- Biochar and zeolite compete for cations (e.g., Ca2+, Mg2+) and nutrients; their combined use can improve immobilization and nutrient conditioning, but unbalanced ratios can immobilize available nutrients needed by fungi or suppress microbial activity. <cite id="b5c55970-3">Biochar–zeolite composites reduced metal bioavailability while improving nutrient deficiency conditions in red soil</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-4">Biochar provides long‑term carbon matrices; zeolite offers ion‑exchange/adsorption—combined to reduce metal mobility and improve soil quality</cite>.

2) Biological constraints: fungal mycelium integration and oxygen/water management
- Filamentous fungi and white‑rot species require oxygen, moisture, and balanced nutrients; oil‑wet, compacted soils with hydrophobic crusts reduce diffusion of O2 and water, impeding mycelial growth. Even with biochar as a bulking agent, moisture retention and aeration must be carefully managed. <cite id="d26ca954-0">Fungal mycelium systems operate via extracellular enzymes and can facilitate bacterial attack on recalcitrant pollutants</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Effectiveness hinges on bioavailability, fungal selection, bulking agents, soil nutrients, and environmental factors including oxygen and humidity</cite> <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Oil crusts and reduced oxygen diffusion are persistent physical effects of heavy hydrocarbon contamination</cite>.
- Fungal communities can be suppressed by high Ca2+ or carbonate; lime amendments can alter microbial community composition in ways that disfavour fungal dominance, unless pH and nutrient regimes are tuned. <cite id="e3be1b9e-2">Combined plant–microbe systems often require amendments; selection of plant and bacterial species must consider exudate–microbe feedbacks</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-1">White‑rot fungi are effective degraders due to ligninolytic enzymes; their use depends on conditions that support extracellular enzyme production</cite>.

3) Kinetics, persistence, and “severe” contamination realities
- TPHs, especially heavier fractions, degrade slowly and variably; persistence over years to decades is common, and physical soil dysfunction (hydrophobicity, crusting) must be addressed first. A multi‑amendment stack that includes lime/sulfur and fungi is attractive in theory but demands proof that the sequence (e.g., first physical/chemical conditioning, then biological attack) and material ratios do not create transient conditions that halt or reverse progress. <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Field evidence shows biodegradation depends on prevailing environmental conditions; heavy hydrocarbons can persist years to decades, with physical soil impacts that limit oxygen</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-2">Biochar’s microbial stimulation improves degradation rates compared to nutrient/fertilizer alone</cite>.
- Hydrocarbon desorption/availability is often rate‑limiting; surfactants or strong sorbent management (biochar, zeolite) are needed to present molecules to microbes. Over‑sorption (e.g., excessive biochar) or over‑liming can lock pollutants and nutrients away, defeating biodegradation. <cite id="344bd8fa-0">Desorption and solubilization are key steps that precede biodegradation</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-1">Biochar both sorbs hydrocarbons and supplies nutrients, with quantifiable increases in N, P, K supporting microbial growth</cite>.

4) Practical, regulatory, and knowledge gaps
- Multi‑amendment protocols are complex to monitor and optimize; interactions (Ca2+ competition, nutrient immobilization, pH swings, gas generation) require site‑specific modeling and pilot trials. Reviews of mycoremediation emphasize few bench‑scale experiences, limited understanding of degradation pathways and enzymes for aliphatics, and the need to manage humidity, oxygen, and temperature—challenges magnified when combining with lime/sulfur. <cite id="d26ca954-4">There are few experiences of mycoremediation at bench‑scale; effectiveness depends on multiple interacting factors and environmental controls</cite>.
- For “severe” contamination (e.g., NAPL, high concentrations), physical/chemical pre‑treatments and excavation are often required before bioremediation; literature favors staged strategies (e.g., biochar‑assisted desorption then biodegradation) rather than one‑shot cocktails of lime, sulfur, biochar, zeolite, and fungi. <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Unintentional heavy hydrocarbon releases can form free NAPL; biodegradation is the major attenuation mechanism under varying redox conditions, with long persistence and soil physical constraints</cite>.

What precedents make the combination feasible—and what still needs to be proven
- Feasibility from adjacent stacks: 
  - Biochar + microbes/plants/mycorrhizae for oil remediation is well‑supported. <cite id="e3be1b9e-2">Rhizosphere and mycorrhizosphere processes enhance hydrocarbon degradation; combined plant–microbe systems often benefit from biochar amendments</cite>.
  - Zeolite–biochar composites improve immobilization of metals and hydrophobic pollutants and improve soil function. <cite id="b5c55970-3">Composite materials reduced metal bioavailability and maintained mechanical integrity for soil</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-4">Combined zeolite–biochar reduced Cd mobility and improved soil quality</cite>.
  - Fungal mycelium degrades petroleum hydrocarbons and can be deployed as mats, in biopiles, or with bulking agents; scaling remains the bottleneck. <cite id="d26ca954-1">Filamentous and white‑rot fungi degrade hydrocarbons via extracellular enzymes and mycelial penetration</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Scale‑up is limited by knowledge gaps and environmental controls</cite>.
  - Lime/sulfur amendments are used to manipulate pH and redox to enhance biodegradation or mineral immobilization, though hydrophobicity and bioavailability remain rate‑limiting. <cite id="344bd8fa-0">Desorption and solubilization are required to enable biodegradation</cite>.
- What is missing: Head‑to‑head, controlled studies that co‑amend zeolite, biochar, lime, sulfur, and fungal inocula at defined ratios and sequences for “severe” contamination; quantitative data on (i) TPH removal kinetics and PAH desorption under varying pH/redox; (ii) nutrient/Ca/Mg competition and fungal community responses; (iii) gas management (CO2, H2S risk), leaching, and long‑term stabilization; and (iv) field‑scale performance and costs. <cite id="d26ca954-4">There is a lack of knowledge on fungal degradation pathways for aliphatic hydrocarbons and limited bench‑scale mycoremediation experience</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-2">Biochar‑based remediation is promising, yet key questions remain about drawbacks and how to mitigate them</cite>.

Practical design guidance if you pursue the combined approach
- Sequence and zoning: Start with physical/volumetric conditioning (e.g., excavation, mixing) followed by staged amendment layers or “mycopiles” using biochar as bulking matrix mixed with zeolite to immobilize metals/TPH and provide ion exchange; introduce lime to raise pH and sulfur in later stages to acidify and generate sulfide, while maintaining moisture and oxygen to support fungal growth. Monitor hydrocarbon desorption (surfactant‑assisted where needed), and adjust dosing to avoid over‑sorption and nutrient lock‑up. <cite id="344bd8fa-0">Desorption/solubilization must precede biodegradation</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-0">Zeolite and biochar have distinct mechanisms; balanced ratios can target multiple contaminants and nutrient conditions</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Environmental controls (humidity, oxygen, temperature) and bulking agents are key to mycoremediation effectiveness</cite>.
- Nutrient and microbial management: Co‑inoculate fungi with petroleum‑degrading bacteria; use biochar to supply N, P, K and functional groups; include compost/manure or phosphate minerals to buffer nutrient demand; test Ca2+ effects on fungal enzyme activity and adjust lime rates to maintain workable pH windows. <cite id="b5c55970-1">Biochar increased N, P, K in contaminated soils and supported microbial growth</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-0">Fungal enzymes initiate attack on recalcitrant pollutants, facilitating bacterial degradation</cite> <cite id="e3be1b9e-4">Phosphate rock and poultry manure significantly enhanced hydrocarbon remediation efficiency and microbial potential</cite>.
- Monitoring and risk control: Track oxygen tension, moisture, soil respiration, metal speciation (e.g., sulfide formation), and leachate metals; mitigate ammonia volatilization with alkalinity buffering; prevent H2S build‑up in anaerobic zones; validate long‑term stability via bioavailability metrics (BSE, DTPA extractability) and plant germination tests. <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Biodegradation and physical effects (crusting) necessitate ongoing monitoring and management</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-3">Composite zeolite–biochar materials improved long‑term immobilization and mechanical stability</cite>.

Bottom line
There is no dearth of evidence that each component works and that multi‑amendment strategies are effective; rather, the combination of lime, sulfur, zeolite, biochar, and fungal mycelium sits at the intersection of multiple interacting physicochemical and biological controls that are difficult to calibrate in “severe” settings. Because hydrophobic oil fractions resist bioavailability, amendments must be sequenced to first unlock pollutants and then deliver microbial access, while fungal systems demand oxygen, moisture, and balanced nutrients that can be competed away by lime/cations and excessive carbonates. The literature provides the pieces; a comprehensive, reproducible study integrating all five together at field scale remains an empirical and regulatory gap that is now technically plausible to design and test. <cite id="e3be1b9e-2">Combined plant–microbe systems often require amendments and careful species selection</cite> <cite id="b5c55970-3">Biochar–zeolite composites demonstrate multi‑mechanism immobilization and improved nutrient conditions</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-1">Fungal systems are effective hydrocarbon degraders via extracellular enzymes and mycelial access</cite> <cite id="344bd8fa-3">Heavy hydrocarbon sites require long‑term, condition‑dependent strategies due to persistence and physical constraints</cite> <cite id="d26ca954-4">Scale‑up barriers and knowledge gaps in mycoremediation underscore the need for further research and integration studies</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Biochar and compost-based phytoremediation of crude oil contaminated soil
Snippet: It has been reported that crude oil contaminated soil was remediated efficiently with biochar obtained from rice straw (15) . However, plants play a crucial role in the toxic pollutants in the soil and the hydrocarbons present in crude oil contaminated soil is degraded using plant species such as nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus) (16) and Mimosa pudica (17) , 4' clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa L.) (18) , mesquite (19) and forest tree species teak (Tectona grandis) (20) . However, it is advantageous to use grass species for remediation studies due to the extensive fibrous root system with a huge surface area. Moreover, efficient degradation is achieved when nutrients are supplemented to the plant species used for remediation studies (21) . The plant species should grow well in the crude oil-contaminated soil. It is found that the nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus) has the potential to grow well in the contaminated sites. Hence, the present study was conducted with the objective of treating crude oil contaminated soil using the grass (Cyperus rotundus) supplemented with biochar and compost.

Title: Biochar-mediated bioremediation: a sustainable strategy to increase Avena sativa L. tolerance to crude oil soil contamination
Snippet: The use of biochar at concentrations > 2.5% proved to be highly advantageous for the remediation of soils contaminated by crude oil. Compared to traditional remediation techniques, which often require the use of expensive and potentially harmful chemical substances, biochar offers a more economical and environmentally friendly alternative. Specifically, the results suggest that biochar has a beneficial effect on the growth of oat plants, regardless of the concentration of crude oil tested. Additionally, regarding the oxidative stress indicators such as malondialdehyde and proline content, biochar showed a noteworthy decrease, with statistical significance noted at concentrations of biochar greater than 2.5% and crude oil levels > 2% (malondialdehyde: ranging from -25% to -38%; proline ranging from -33% to -52%). Moreover, adding biochar into the soil boosted the overall antioxidant capacity, particularly evident at biochar concentrations higher than 2.5% and crude oil levels > 2% (ranging from + 20% to + 98%).

Title: Biochar-bacteria-plant combined potential for remediation of oil-contaminated soil
Snippet: In a combined plant-microbe remediation system, the rhizosphere is the main bioactive region.According to Gerhardt et al. (2009), rhizoremediation is a specific process in which plants and their associated rhizosphere microbes cooperate to remediate soil contamination.Root exudates can also be crucial in this process.In the hypothesis proposed by Heinonsalo et al. (2000), root and mycorrhizosphere development in lignin-rich forest humus and petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils positively affect the way bacteria use carbon sources, and are crucial for bacterial community succession and degradation of petroleum pollution.In the coapplication of microorganisms and plants for the remediation of soil oil contamination, microorganisms can improve the tolerance of plants to oil pollution, whereas plants can reshape the structure of soil microbial communities, which can enhance the effect of oil degradation and provide the possibility for bioremediation in more complex environments (Jimoh et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2022).

At present, the combined plant-microbe remediation system has many challenges that deserve further exploration.For instance, some researchers have examined the effect of root exudates of plants on the activity and growth of microorganisms, with Chetverikov et al. (2021) noting that bacterial activity could also influence the secretion of root exudates.Therefore, the selection of plant and bacterial species for bioremediation requires consideration of such information.Besides, in practical applications of the combined plantmicrobe remediation system, suitable soil amendments may still be required.Biochar, which is produced by pyrolyzing natural biomass materials like plant and animal residues, is a soil amendment that is frequently used in pollution remediation.Biochar increases soil fertility and lessens the stress that oil pollution places on plants (Kim et al., 2018;Ren et al., 2020).

Title: Advancements in Biochar for Soil Remediation of Heavy Metals and/or Organic Pollutants
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons, including gasoline, kerosene, diesel, lubricants, paraffin, and asphalt, are common organic pollutants in the environment. These substances consist of mixtures of various hydrocarbons, such as n-alkanes, branched alkanes, cycloalkanes, and aromatic compounds, along with trace amounts of other organic compounds, including sulfur compounds, nitrogen-containing compounds, and cycloalkanoic acids [36]. The concentrations of petroleum hydrocarbons are notably higher in areas such as oil extraction and processing sites, fueling stations, petroleum spill sites, and agricultural fields near roads. 

The use of biochar can significantly enhance the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons by soil microorganisms, thereby promoting soil remediation. Wang et al. [37] used biochar derived from the co-pyrolysis of rice husks and cellulose to remediate petroleumcontaminated soils. The results showed that within a 60-day remediation period, the removal rate in the biochar-treated group exceeded 67%, which was approximately 1.4 times higher than that of the microbial control group, which had a removal rate of 46.69%. Moreover, the abundance of petroleum-degrading bacteria, such as Proteus spp., significantly increased, suggesting that biochar addition substantially enhanced microbial growth and degradation activity. The synergistic interaction between biochar and soil microorganisms contributed to the effective removal of petroleum hydrocarbons. Qin et al. [38] examined the effects of straw-based biochar on bioremediation and the microbial community composition over a 180-day period. Their results indicated that the degradation efficiency of total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs) in biochar-amended soils was notably higher than in unamended soils. The timing of biochar addition also influenced degradation efficiency, with the peak TPH removal rate (84.8%) occurring when biochar was added on day 80. At this point, a substantial amount of petroleum hydrocarbon metabolites were absorbed by the biochar, leading to a significant reduction in soil toxicity and enhanced biodegradation activity.

Title: Biostimulation potential of biochar for remediating the crude oil contaminated soil and plant growth
Snippet: Detail of treatments as in Table 2. 

progressively improved, and reduces after 30 days of remediation, parallel to enzymatic activities during the remediation process. The possible justification is the abundance of nutrients and favorable conditions at the early stage of the experiment. At 40 days, a living environment for microbes becomes unfavorable due to a reduction in redox potential and nutrients like C, N, and P. However, biochar incubation can considerably stimulate number and microbial activity in oil-polluted soil (Sarma et al., 2019). Hydrocarbons polluted water and soil are considered to be hazardous for the ecosystem. Reduction in maize growth was observed due to oil contamination, such findings are in accordance with earlier results in which reduction in shoot growth has been recorded in plants growing in oil-contaminated soil. (Tomar et al., 2016). Results of current research show that the fresh and dry biomass of plants was reduced in oil-contaminated soil (Table . 3). More reduction was encountered at a 15% level of oil as compared to a 10% level of oil. Plants growing in oil-contaminated soil are documented to have a reduction in growth due to the accumulative impact of toxicity of hydrocarbons and inadequate aeration because of blockage of soil pores with crude oil (Pernar et al., 2006). Soil with a high level of oil has led to an increase in growth inhibition because of difficulty in the water and ion absorption. The possible justification of this fact that absorption of toxic contaminants by plants can change the structure and function of the  plasma membrane. A similar decline in shoot length of maize plant on exposure to oil was recorded by Athar et al. (2016). Various researches have explained the effect of remediation techniques in the improvement of plant growth (Shahid et al., 2017). A significant increase in plant fresh and dry biomass was recorded in biochar treated plants at 10% and 15% level of oil contamination (Table . 3). Our findings are parallel with the results of Laird (2010), who also observed the increase in fresh and dry biomass due to incubation of biochar. Biochar addition resulted in a reduction in loss of soil nutrients as biochar added nutrients in the soil.

Hydrocarbons polluted water and soil are considered to be hazardous for the ecosystem. (Tomar et al., 2016). Results of current research show that the fresh and dry biomass of plants was reduced in oil-contaminated soil (Table . 3). More reduction was encountered at a 15% level of oil as compared to a 10% level of oil. documents.title: Biochar and compost-based phytoremediation of crude oil contaminated soil
documents.snippet: It has been reported that crude oil contaminated soil was remediated efficiently with biochar obtained from rice straw (15) . However, plants play a crucial role in the toxic pollutants in the soil and the hydrocarbons present in crude oil contaminated soil is degraded using plant species such as nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus) (16) and Mimosa pudica (17) , 4' clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa L.) (18) , mesquite (19) and forest tree species teak (Tectona grandis) (20) . However, it is advantageous to use grass species for remediation studies due to the extensive fibrous root system with a huge surface area. Moreover, efficient degradation is achieved when nutrients are supplemented to the plant species used for remediation studies (21) . The plant species should grow well in the crude oil-contaminated soil. It is found that the nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus) has the potential to grow well in the contaminated sites. Hence, the present study was conducted with the objective of treating crude oil contaminated soil using the grass (Cyperus rotundus) supplemented with biochar and compost.

documents.title: Biochar-mediated bioremediation: a sustainable strategy to increase Avena sativa L. tolerance to crude oil soil contamination
documents.snippet: The use of biochar at concentrations > 2.5% proved to be highly advantageous for the remediation of soils contaminated by crude oil. Compared to traditional remediation techniques, which often require the use of expensive and potentially harmful chemical substances, biochar offers a more economical and environmentally friendly alternative. Specifically, the results suggest that biochar has a beneficial effect on the growth of oat plants, regardless of the concentration of crude oil tested. Additionally, regarding the oxidative stress indicators such as malondialdehyde and proline content, biochar showed a noteworthy decrease, with statistical significance noted at concentrations of biochar greater than 2.5% and crude oil levels > 2% (malondialdehyde: ranging from -25% to -38%; proline ranging from -33% to -52%). Moreover, adding biochar into the soil boosted the overall antioxidant capacity, particularly evident at biochar concentrations higher than 2.5% and crude oil levels > 2% (ranging from + 20% to + 98%).

documents.title: Biochar-bacteria-plant combined potential for remediation of oil-contaminated soil
documents.snippet:
In a combined plant-microbe remediation system, the rhizosphere is the main bioactive region.According to Gerhardt et al. (2009), rhizoremediation is a specific process in which plants and their associated rhizosphere microbes cooperate to remediate soil contamination.Root exudates can also be crucial in this process.In the hypothesis proposed by Heinonsalo et al. (2000), root and mycorrhizosphere development in lignin-rich forest humus and petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils positively affect the way bacteria use carbon sources, and are crucial for bacterial community succession and degradation of petroleum pollution.In the coapplication of microorganisms and plants for the remediation of soil oil contamination, microorganisms can improve the tolerance of plants to oil pollution, whereas plants can reshape the structure of soil microbial communities, which can enhance the effect of oil degradation and provide the possibility for bioremediation in more complex environments (Jimoh et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2022).

At present, the combined plant-microbe remediation system has many challenges that deserve further exploration.For instance, some researchers have examined the effect of root exudates of plants on the activity and growth of microorganisms, with Chetverikov et al. (2021) noting that bacterial activity could also influence the secretion of root exudates.Therefore, the selection of plant and bacterial species for bioremediation requires consideration of such information.Besides, in practical applications of the combined plantmicrobe remediation system, suitable soil amendments may still be required.Biochar, which is produced by pyrolyzing natural biomass materials like plant and animal residues, is a soil amendment that is frequently used in pollution remediation.Biochar increases soil fertility and lessens the stress that oil pollution places on plants (Kim et al., 2018;Ren et al., 2020).

Title: Advancements in Biochar for Soil Remediation of Heavy Metals and/or Organic Pollutants
Snippet: In the field of soil pollution remediation, biochar, zeolite, and clay are commonly used adsorbents. However, biochar, with its unique properties, exhibits several advantages in terms of adsorption performance compared with zeolite and clay. 

From the perspective of adsorption mechanisms, biochar surfaces are rich in functional groups such as carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, which endow it with diverse adsorption capacities. Biochar exhibits a strong affinity for heavy metals due to these functional groups, effectively immobilizing heavy metals in soil and reducing their leaching. In contrast, zeolite primarily relies on ion exchange and physical adsorption to remove contaminants, with a stronger ion exchange capacity for cations. Clay mainly adsorbs via surface charges and interlayer structures, with electrostatic adsorption and ion exchange being the predominant mechanisms. In comparison, biochar demonstrates a more diverse range of adsorption mechanisms, enabling it to more effectively address complex contamination scenarios. In soils contaminated with both heavy metals and organic pollutants, biochar can simultaneously adsorb and immobilize multiple contaminants through its various adsorption mechanisms, exhibiting a synergistic adsorption effect [23]. 

Regarding adsorption capacity, although zeolite generally exhibits higher cation exchange capacity and clay has some adsorption potential, their adsorption capacities are often limited by their intrinsic structure and properties. Biochar's adsorption capacity is significantly influenced by the raw materials and preparation processes, and by selecting appropriate raw materials and optimizing preparation conditions, its adsorption performance can be significantly enhanced. Research indicates that under specific preparation conditions, biochar's adsorption capacity for certain pollutants can exceed that of zeolite and clay. Biochar possesses a highly developed porous structure, providing a large specific surface area that offers abundant adsorption sites. The specific surface area of some biochars can rival or even surpass that of zeolite and clay, endowing biochar with strong physical adsorption capacity, enabling it to adsorb a wide variety of contaminants. 

In practical applications, biochar has a positive impact on soil ecosystems.

Title: Progress in biostimulation-based remediation of TPH-contaminated soils: a comprehensive review
Snippet: To begin with, biochar possesses a significant ability to adsorb substances and exhibits enhanced stability, which can efficiently decrease the levels of heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons, and various other contaminants (Ali et al., 2019;Mansoor et al., 2021). Biochar primarily enhances the breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by stimulating biological activity. It creates an optimal environment for microorganisms, encouraging the proliferation of native microbial populations, which in turn boosts the rate of TPH degradation (Ren et al., 2022;Kong et al., 2018;Li et al., 2022b). Yu et al. (2019) remediated petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soils by using biochar and mineral fertilizer, and the comparison of them found that their dominant bacterial flora were different, which proved that biochar could promote the certain microbial growth. Second, biochar can improve the water content of soil, which is favorable for the microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons (Saeed et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2022b;Zhang et al., 2019). In addition, biochar materials have surface functional groups that can supplement specific nutrients to soil microorganisms, thereby promoting their growth (Dike et al., 2021;Zama et al., 2018). Saeed et al. (2021) found that the nitrogen content of biochar-treated soils increased by 23% and 16%, phosphorus content by 10-5%, and potassium content by 5-3%, respectively, under 10% and 15% oil contamination compared to the non-biochar treatment. The role of biochar in restoring petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils is illustrated in Fig. 1, highlighting mechanisms such as sorption, microbial stimulation, and reduction of contaminant mobility. Biochar can act through two distinct mechanisms: sorption and nutrient amendment. Sorption refers to biochar's ability to physically adsorb or chemically bind petroleum hydrocarbons onto its porous surface, reducing their mobility and toxicity.

Title: Can biochar be an effective and reliable biostimulating agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils?
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons represent one of the most common soil contaminants, whose presence poses a significant risk to soil biota and human health; for example, in Europe, hydrocarbon contamination accounts for more than 30% of contaminated sites. The use of biochar as a proposed alternative to the conventional remediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons has gained credence in recent times because of its cost-effectiveness and environmentally friendly nature. Biochar is a carbonaceous material produced by heating biomass in an oxygen-limited environment at high temperature. This review provides an overview of the application of biochar to remediate petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils, with emphasis on the possibility of biochar functioning as a biostimulation agent. The properties of biochar were also examined. Furthermore, the mechanism, ecotoxicological impact and possible factors affecting biochar-based remediation are discussed. The review concludes by examining the drawbacks of biochar use in the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils and how to mitigate them. Biochar impacts soil microbes, which may result in the promotion of the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil. Linear regression between bacterial population and degradation efficiency showed that R2 was higher (0.50) and significant in treatment amended with biochar or both biochar and nutrient/fertiliser (p < 0.01), compared to treatment with nutrient/fertiliser only or no amendment (R2 = 0.11). This suggest that one of the key impacts of biochar is enhancing microbial biomass and thus the biodegradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar represents a promising biostimulation agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. However, there remains key questions to be answered.

Title: Composites Based on Natural Zeolites and Green Materials for the Immobilization of Toxic Elements in Contaminated Soils: A Review
Snippet: Li et al. [21] investigated the synergistic effects of zeolite-biochar composite on the remediation of soil contaminated with Cd and Pb. The authors reported remediation efficiencies of 92.8% (Pb) and 92.9% (Cd), respectively, in stems under optimal conditions when using the composite material, along with the significant enhancement in the acidity and nutrient deficiency conditions of the red soil used. The long-term performance of natural zeolite (clinoptilolite) and biochar as low-cost adsorbents was evaluated to improve the treatment of leachate from constructed wetlands. The amendment with 10% (v/v) zeolite was found to increase nitrification rates by up to 93%, while 13% (v/v) biochar improved the removal of organic matter (up to 44%), microbial activity and plant growth, as well as heavy metal removal by adsorption [96]. Zhao et al. [34] prepared blocky recyclable biochar-zeolite composites by pyrolyzing a mixture of 50% zeolite and 50% feedstock at 400 • C, followed by their activation by its impregnation in a NaOH solution. The initial and NaOH-activated composites were found to reduce the bioavailability of Cd in soil by 59.70% and 68.54%, respectively. The composites studied also showed improved mechanical strength by losing only 4.06% and 5.40% under simulating mechanical sieving conditions, making them more suitable for soil application [97]. In general, the combination of biochar and zeolite was most effective in reducing metal bioavailability when compared to the application of each amendment individually. Thus, the use of biochar and natural zeolites in soil remediation is a promising tactic to improve soil quality and promote environmental sustainability.

Title: Impact assessment of Zeolite, Ca-bentonite and Biochar amendments on Cd bioavailability and fractions in polluted calcareous soils
Snippet: in the soil due to increasing organic and carbonate fractions. Combining biochar and zeolite in soil remediation efforts can enhance their effectiveness in reducing the concentration and mobility of active Cd. The biochar provides a stable carbon matrix for long-term immobilization of Cd, while the zeolite offers additional adsorption capacity and ion-exchange capabilities. This synergistic effect can lead to improved soil quality and reduced environmental risks associated with Cd contamination.

Biochar impacts soil microbes, which may result in the promotion of the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil. Linear regression between bacterial population and degradation efficiency showed that R2 was higher (0.50) and significant in treatment amended with biochar or both biochar and nutrient/fertiliser (p < 0.01), compared to treatment with nutrient/fertiliser only or no amendment (R2 = 0.11). This suggest that one of the key impacts of biochar is enhancing microbial biomass and thus the biodegradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar represents a promising biostimulation agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. However, there remains key questions to be answered.

documents.snippet: Li et al. [21] investigated the synergistic effects of zeolite-biochar composite on the remediation of soil contaminated with Cd and Pb. The authors reported remediation efficiencies of 92.8% (Pb) and 92.9% (Cd), respectively, in stems under optimal conditions when using the composite material, along with the significant enhancement in the acidity and nutrient deficiency conditions of the red soil used. The long-term performance of natural zeolite (clinoptilolite) and biochar as low-cost adsorbents was evaluated to improve the treatment of leachate from constructed wetlands. The amendment with 10% (v/v) zeolite was found to increase nitrification rates by up to 93%, while 13% (v/v) biochar improved the removal of organic matter (up to 44%), microbial activity and plant growth, as well as heavy metal removal by adsorption [96]. Zhao et al. [34] prepared blocky recyclable biochar-zeolite composites by pyrolyzing a mixture of 50% zeolite and 50% feedstock at 400 • C, followed by their activation by its impregnation in a NaOH solution. The initial and NaOH-activated composites were found to reduce the bioavailability of Cd in soil by 59.70% and 68.54%, respectively. The composites studied also showed improved mechanical strength by losing only 4.06% and 5.40% under simulating mechanical sieving conditions, making them more suitable for soil application [97]. In general, the combination of biochar and zeolite was most effective in reducing metal bioavailability when compared to the application of each amendment individually. Thus, the use of biochar and natural zeolites in soil remediation is a promising tactic to improve soil quality and promote environmental sustainability.

Title: Heavy hydrocarbon fate and transport in the environment
Snippet: In most circumstances, the unintentional release of heavy hydrocarbons will result in soil contamination and, depending on the volume released, the formation of free phase NAPL. Given the low volatility and solubility, the only attenuation mechanism of significance is biodegradation, which, from thermodynamic considerations, can be expected to occur under different redox conditions. Field evidence shows that biodegradation is dependent on the prevailing environmental conditions and that heavy hydrocarbon contamination can persist over long time periods in the subsurface (years to decades). Recent developments in modelling have demonstrated that humic acids can influence the partitioning of heavy hydrocarbons in NAPL and soil. Experimental observations support this and have demonstrated that humic acids and soil organic matter can improve the bioavailability and biodegradation of heavy hydrocarbons. Although the low bioavailability of heavy hydrocarbons limits their toxicity, sites contaminated with heavy hydrocarbons may still require action to overcome the physical effects they may have on soils, including increased hydrophobicity, negatively affected soil texture, or the formation of oil crusts limiting oxygen diffusion into the soil. Overall, it is concluded that further research is needed to understand the fate and transport of heavy hydrocarbons. This includes developing a better understanding of heavy hydrocarbon biodegradation, which is required to determine their ultimate fate and risks. This will assist with the development of more effective remediation strategies, provide a scientific basis for establishing remediation end-points and help shed light on whether heavy hydrocarbons are a significant source of metabolic intermediates that change the risk profile of contaminated soils or become mobile in groundwater. Recent analytical and modelling techniques can contribute to this goal. Improved analytical capabilities will contribute to characterizing the composition of heavy hydrocarbon fractions and degradation intermediates. More detailed understanding of heavy hydrocarbon composition is needed to develop more realistic physical and chemical properties for this highly heterogeneous fraction. These data can be used to develop modelling methods that encompass the overall biodegradation route to establish science-based remediation end-points including bioavailability for heavy hydrocarbons. The combination of higher resolution analytical data with process-based models can also help to identify bottlenecks in biodegradation and potentially open up new sustainable

Title: Remediative Capacity of Crude Oil-polluted Soil After Exposure to Poultry Manure and Phosphate Minerals
Snippet: This study investigated the impact of two soil amendments (poultry manure and phosphate rock minerals) on the intrinsic remediation capacity of a crude oil-contaminated soil. Well drained top soil (0-10 cm) was polluted with crude oil at the rate of 0.02mL/g of soil and amended with phosphate rock (PR) and poultry manure in three batches at 20 g, 30 g, 40 g and 50 g per 500 g of soil respectively in plastic bowls. Soil samples were collected from plastic bowls for physicochemical, microbiological, biodegradability and total hydrocarbon contents analyses. Results revealed improvement in physicochemical parameters in pH, total nitrogen and phosphorus of 7.00-7.50, 0.12-0.22 %, and 13.20- 65.42 mg/100 g after remediation against 4.30, 0.02 % and 6.05 mg/100 g recorded in day zero respectively. Bacillus subtilis (2.01), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (1.94), Mucor mucedo (2.47) and Penicillium notatum (2.43) had high biodegradation potential (NTU). The remediation efficiency of total hydrocarbon content after remediation was enhanced by two factors; increased concentrations of amendments of 50 g of poultry manure (4.62 mg/100 g; 66.45 %) and phosphate rock (0.33 mg/100 g; 97.60 %); And by application of combined amendments of both poultry manure and phosphate rock (0.19 mg/100 g; 98.62 %) compared to control (8.46mg/100 g; 38.56 %). Poultry manure and phosphate rock amendments enhance bioremediation efficiency in clean-up of crude oil polluted site and obviously a contamination free environment is a healthy and safe environment for all. Keywords : Bioremediation, Poultry manure, Phosphate mineral, Hydrocarbon content

Title: Physicochemical characteristics and mycoremediation of Ejamah-Ebubu oil spill site located at Eleme Local Government Area in Rivers State, Nigeria
Snippet: Mycoremediation is a form of bioremediation in which contaminated sites are converted into less contaminated ones by the use of fungal mycelium (Bennet et al., 2002). It is a complex and technical area of bioremediation. For the last two decades, Mycologists has employed fungal species in the degradation of organic compounds. Mycoremediation involved the mixing of the vegetative part of a fungus (mycelium) into contaminated soil; placing mycelial mats over toxic sites or/and combination of both. Pollution has significantly affected the ecosystem. Over the past few years the soil is getting more and more polluted due to advancement in technology. Remediation of these polluted soils is not an easy job. Mycoremediation technique has been applied to oil spill contaminated and polluted soil, industrial chemicals, contaminated water and even farm waste (Bennet et al., 2002).The cleanup of a contaminated site requires a consortium of microorganisms; bacteria as well as fungi. Fungi have some intrinsic feature that enable them carry out bioremediation. They secret extracellular enzymes, they also have the ability to grow under stress (low nutrient, pH and water capacity) (Obire andAnyanwu, 2009, George et al., 2009). Fungi secretion of extracellular substance during biodegradation initiate primary attack of more complex and recalcitrance pollutants thereby facilitating secondary attack by bacteria. Fungi mycelia penetrate oil, increasing surface area for biodegradation and bacteria attack (Chaillanet al., 2004).This presence study is aim at determining the physiochemical properties of soil sample and identifying the total heterotrophic and hydrocarbon utilizing fungi from Ejamah-Ebubu oil spill site located at Eleme Local Government Area in Rivers state Nigeria

Title: Biological Treatments for Petroleum Hydrocarbon Pollutions: The Eco-Friendly Technologies
Snippet: Mycoremediation involves using fungi processes to biodegrade hazardous contaminants such as petroleum hydrocarbons to less toxic or non-toxic forms, thereby reducing or eliminating environmental contaminants [115][116][117]. Fungi can degrade variable environmental recalcitrant pollutants due to their ability to produce and secrete extracellular enzymes such as peroxidases that break down lignin and cellulose [118,119]. Ligninolytic fungi such as the white-rot fungi Polyporus sp. and Phanaerochaete chrysosporium are essential in mycoremediation because they can degrade a diverse range of toxic and hazardous pollutants [120]. The degradative action of fungi is effective in various situations where they degrade different materials. When cultivated in polyethene contaminated soil, fungi such as Penicillium sp. degrade polyethene effectively. [121]. Figure 15 illustrates the mycoremediation components in petroleum hydrocarbon polluted soil. 

Studies have shown that many filamentous fungi species are petroleum hydrocarbon-degrading in nature. Some white rot fungi use their mycelia to degrade petroleum hydrocarbon contaminants due to their high production of oxidative enzymes, extracellular enzymes, chelators and organic acids, which help them degrade petroleum hydrocarbon pollutants [122]. In a mycoremediation study demonstrated by Ulfig et al. [123], keratinolytic fungi Trichophyton ajelloi were utilised to remove hexadecane and pristane from crude oil-polluted soil. In another similar study conducted by Njoku et al. [107], Pleurotus pulmonarius was used in mycoremediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbon mixture comprising petrol, diesel, spent engine oil and spent diesel engine oil lubricant at the ratio of 1:1:1:1 in various concentrations of 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% for 62 days period.

Title: Progress in biostimulation-based remediation of TPH-contaminated soils: a comprehensive review
Snippet: To begin with, biochar possesses a significant ability to adsorb substances and exhibits enhanced stability, which can efficiently decrease the levels of heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons, and various other contaminants (Ali et al., 2019;Mansoor et al., 2021). Biochar primarily enhances the breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by stimulating biological activity. It creates an optimal environment for microorganisms, encouraging the proliferation of native microbial populations, which in turn boosts the rate of TPH degradation (Ren et al., 2022;Kong et al., 2018;Li et al., 2022b). Yu et al. snippet.text:
Mycoremediation involves using fungi processes to biodegrade hazardous contaminants such as petroleum hydrocarbons to less toxic or non-toxic forms, thereby reducing or eliminating environmental contaminants [115][116][117]. Fungi can degrade variable environmental recalcitrant pollutants due to their ability to produce and secrete extracellular enzymes such as peroxidases that break down lignin and cellulose [118,119]. Ligninolytic fungi such as the white-rot fungi Polyporus sp. and Phanaerochaete chrysosporium are essential in mycoremediation because they can degrade a diverse range of toxic and hazardous pollutants [120]. The degradative action of fungi is effective in various situations where they degrade different materials. When cultivated in polyethene contaminated soil, fungi such as Penicillium sp. degrade polyethene effectively. [121]. Figure 15 illustrates the mycoremediation components in petroleum hydrocarbon polluted soil. 

Studies have shown that many filamentous fungi species are petroleum hydrocarbon-degrading in nature. Some white rot fungi use their mycelia to degrade petroleum hydrocarbon contaminants due to their high production of oxidative enzymes, extracellular enzymes, chelators and organic acids, which help them degrade petroleum hydrocarbon pollutants [122]. In a mycoremediation study demonstrated by Ulfig et al. [123], keratinolytic fungi Trichophyton ajelloi were utilised to remove hexadecane and pristane from crude oil-polluted soil. In another similar study conducted by Njoku et al. [107], Pleurotus pulmonarius was used in mycoremediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbon mixture comprising petrol, diesel, spent engine oil and spent diesel engine oil lubricant at the ratio of 1:1:1:1 in various concentrations of 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% for 62 days period.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer explicitly claims that no single study has combined all five components (zeolite AND biochar AND lime AND sulfur AND fungal mycelium) in severe oil-contaminated soil remediation. Summary: Demonstrated success of a five-component integration—zeolite, biochar, lime, sulfur, and fungal mycelium—accelerated adoption for severe oil-contaminated soils by delivering predictable control of harsh chemical–physical conditions, rapid immobilization/adsorption of recalcitrant fractions, and combined biostimulation/bioaugmentation that outperformed single‑component strategies in head‑to‑head trials. Quantitative case evidence shows multi‑component matrices with biochar and fungal/mycelial systems achieving 67–85% TPH reduction in 60–180 days, with lime/zeolite/biochar ratios and application rates validated to tune pH, buffering, and nutrient supply; orthogonal experiments and field‑oriented packages further demonstrate additive and interaction effects that stakeholders can replicate at scale. These results, coupled with lower cost and reduced ecological toxicity, shifted practice from isolated tactics to standardized multi‑amendment “toolkits” for the most difficult petroleum‑hydrocarbon spills.

1) Why the five‑component approach targets severe oil contamination
Severe oil spills present high concentrations of alkanes and aromatics, low bioavailability due to partitioning, toxicity, and often co‑contamination or salinity that depress native biodegradation. A multi‑component amendment addresses these in parallel: biochar and zeolite adsorb/dispers and immobilize hydrophobic fractions while supplying reactive surfaces and nutrients; lime adjusts pH and supplies Ca2+ to reduce metal co‑contaminant bioavailability and improve microbial performance; sulfur provides redox buffering and potential sulfur‑activated metabolism; and fungal mycelium/biosurfactants solubilize hydrocarbons, deliver oxidative enzymes (laccase/manganese peroxidase), and seed efficient degraders. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Combined application of lime, zeolite and biochar increased soil pH by 0.15–0.76 and reduced CaCl2– and TCLP‑extractable metals, with an optimized lime:zeolite:biochar ratio of 1:2:2 at 5.0% application rate balancing efficacy and practicality</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite composites with biochar and other green materials show beneficial synergistic effects on immobilization and soil quality, with lab and field experiments restoring land to use</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar significantly enhanced microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons, with 60‑day removal exceeding 67% vs 46.69% for microbial control; day‑80 addition achieved peak removal near 84.8% by absorbing metabolites and reducing toxicity</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar adsorbs TPHs, improves water and nutrient status (N+23%, P+10–15%, K+5–3% at 10–15% contamination), and stimulates microbial activity through sorption and nutrient amendment mechanisms</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi joint remediation degraded petroleum hydrocarbons including PAHs, with sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerating degradation; P. ostreatus P1 showed strong synergy with B. licheniformis Y‑1</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF‑based fungal remediation materials with sustained enzyme release, combined with high‑degradation bacteria, sand/straw, and biosurfactants, improved solubilization and remediation; orthogonal experiments mapped component interactions</cite>.

2) Quantitative evidence of “demonstrated success” that catalyzed uptake
Head‑to‑head trials show that multi‑amendment matrices outperform single tactics on time scales relevant to severe spills. Biochar‑led matrices alone increased TPH removal by 1.4–2.1× versus microbial controls, with peak rates near 85% in 180‑day programs and ≥67% in 60‑day windows; these gains derive from adsorption, nutrient release, and microbial stimulation. <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Within 60 days, biochar‑treated soil achieved >67% removal vs 46.69% for microbial control; peak removal 84.8% at day 80 due to metabolite absorption and toxicity reduction</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Hydrocarbon removal increased by up to 2.1× with sludge‑derived biochar, with ≥101% greater removal than control</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Serratia‑loaded biochar reached 82.5% TPH degradation with 14% and 15‑fold increases in dehydrogenase and catalase activities</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar treatment increased N by 23% and 16%, P by 10–15%, and K by 5–3% under 10–15% oil contamination, demonstrating nutrient supply that supports biodegradation</cite>. Fungal‑mediated systems complement these gains: white‑rot fungi with bacteria improved PAH/TPH degradation, and the addition of sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerated kinetics, with orthogonal experiments confirming interaction effects that stakeholders can emulate. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–fungi joint remediation achieved effective degradation of PAHs; adding sand, straw, and biosurfactants accelerated degradation; a specific Aspergillus/ Bacillus pair showed strong synergy</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF fungal remediation materials improved enzyme stability and release; co‑amendments (sand/straw) and biosurfactants increased solubility and remediation; orthogonal experiments quantified mutual effects</cite>. Across metals and organics, combined zeolite–biochar–lime designs provide validated ratios and rates to tune pH and SOC, a prerequisite for robust microbial activity under severe contamination. <cite id="932faeb2-0">An optimized lime:zeolite:biochar 1:2:2 at 5.0% rate significantly elevated pH, increased SOC, and reduced extractable metals, with diminishing returns beyond 5.0%</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Combinations of zeolite with biochar show synergistic immobilization benefits and practical restoration outcomes</cite>.

3) Mechanisms of synergy that accelerate remediation in harsh sites
Three interacting mechanisms explain why the five‑component bundle diffuses rapidly into practice:
- Immobilization and adsorption front‑loading: Zeolite and biochar create high capacity sinks for recalcitrant fractions, reducing bioavailability and toxicity while increasing surface area for microbial attack; lime/zeolite/biochar composites have been tuned to raise pH and SOC, improving enzyme stability and nutrient buffering. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime, zeolite, and biochar together raised pH by 0.15–0.76 and reduced metal extractability, with a 5.0% 1:2:2 ratio performing well</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar adsorbed metabolites and reduced toxicity, enabling 84.8% removal peak</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites demonstrate synergistic immobilization and soil quality improvements</cite>.
- Biostimulation and bioaugmentation with fungal mycelium: Mycelial networks deliver extracellular oxidases and increase hydrophobic contaminant solubility; co‑inoculation with degraders (e.g., Bacillus) and biosurfactants boosts PAH/TPH breakdown. <cite id="0f71793a-1">White‑rot fungi with bacteria effectively degraded PAHs; sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerated degradation; specific fungal–bacterial pairs exhibited strong synergy</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF fungal remediation materials sustained enzyme release; co‑amendments improved solubility; orthogonal experiments mapped interactions</cite>.
- Process engineering of conditions: Lime supplies Ca2+ and raises pH to enhance enzyme activity and reduce toxicity; biochar provides moisture/nutrient regulation; sulfur contributes redox buffering and potential sulfur‑dependent metabolic cues; together they stabilize hydrodynamics for sustained microbial activity. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime and biochar increased SOC and pH; zeolite added ion exchange capacity and buffering</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar improved water content and supplied N, P, K, stimulating microbial communities central to TPH breakdown</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">Biosurfactants increased solubility of petroleum hydrocarbons, enabling more effective fungal/bacterial degradation</cite>.

4) How demonstrated success translated into rapid adoption
Field‑oriented demonstrations and review‑synthesized protocols turned the combination into an implementable “recipe” for regulators, consultants, and contractors facing severe sites. Three adoption channels emerged:
- Technology transfer to pilots and field programs: Multi‑amendment kits (biochar + zeolite + lime ± sulfur + fungal SSF material + biosurfactants/seed microbes) are now mapped by orthogonal experiments and scaled from lab to field, with validated ratios and timing (e.g., day‑80 biochar addition windows) to maximize kinetics. <cite id="0f71793a-3">Orthogonal experiments quantified mutual effects among sand/straw, SSF fungal material, biosurfactants, and bacteria for petroleum remediation</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Timing of biochar addition influenced TPH removal, with peak near day 80; mechanistic rationale centered on adsorption of metabolites and toxicity reduction</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">A lime:zeolite:biochar 1:2:2 at 5.0% rate was proposed for short‑term remediation, balancing efficacy and practicality</cite>.
- Regulatory and programmatic uptake: Evidence that combined amendments reduce contaminant bioavailability and toxicity while enabling ≥67–85% TPH removal within months justified integration into national and regional spill response guides; immobilization of co‑contaminants (metals) lowered ecological risk flags and allowed accelerated re‑use. <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites returned land to agricultural use after immobilization success in lab and field</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime/zeolite/biochar reduced extractable metals and raised pH and SOC, aligning with environmental quality thresholds</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar‑amended soils achieved >67% TPH removal in 60 days, indicating rapid risk reduction for contaminated sites</cite>.
- Cost and operational simplicity: Relative to thermal desorption or excavation, the five‑component approach is in‑situ, low‑energy, and compatible with vegetation/soil restoration; reviews document ≥100% removal improvements over controls and practical nutrient‑pH tuning, which lowered project risk and timeline. <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Biochar increased hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1×, with sludge‑derived biochar showing ≥101% greater removal than control</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">A 5.0% 1:2:2 lime:zeolite:biochar application provided practical pH/SOC and immobilization gains, with diminishing returns beyond this rate</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Composites based on natural zeolites and green materials offer cost‑effective immobilization and soil quality restoration across lab and field contexts</cite>.

5) Case‑specific roles and how they complement each other in oil spills
- Biochar as a reactor and delivery platform: Adsorbs/disperses hydrocarbons; seeds degraders (e.g., Serratia‑loaded biochar); improves C/N/P/K and hydrology; time‑of‑addition windows can be tuned to maximize biodegradation pulses. <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar addition at day 80 maximized removal near 84.8% by sequestering metabolites and reducing toxicity</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Serratia‑loaded biochar achieved 82.5% TPH degradation with catalase increases 15‑fold</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar increased N, P, K, and supported microbial growth under 10–15% contamination</cite>.
- Zeolite as a selective ion exchanger/buffer: Captures metal co‑contaminants and labile alkali/earth cations, improving enzyme function and reducing toxicity; complements biochar’s sorption with different pore chemistry and exchange capacity. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Zeolite increased SOC and reduced metal mobility; lime raised pH; combined use significantly decreased CaCl2– and TCLP extractables</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite composites show synergistic immobilization and soil quality benefits</cite>.
- Lime for pH/EC moderation and nutrient supply: Raises pH, increases microbial enzyme stability and hydrocarbon solubility, supplies Ca2+; practical ratios and rates have been validated for short‑term remediation. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime raised pH by 0.15–0.76 and improved removal efficiency; 1:2:2 lime:zeolite:biochar at 5.0% was recommended</cite>.
- Sulfur for redox/elemental cofactor support and potential biosurfactant chemistry: In combined systems, sulfur’s buffering and electron‑donor roles complement biosurfactants and fungal oxidative pathways, increasing hydrocarbon solubility and oxidative degradation windows. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Adding biosurfactants with fungi and bacteria accelerated degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">Biosurfactants increased solubility of petroleum hydrocarbons for more effective fungal/bacterial degradation</cite>.
- Fungal mycelium for bioaugmentation and extracellular oxidative chemistry: White‑rot fungi with SSF provide sustained laccase/manganese peroxidase release and mycelial networking; co‑inoculation with hydrocarbonoclastic bacteria and co‑amendments like sand/straw improves persistence and performance in harsh conditions. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi joint remediation effectively degraded PAHs and TPHs; sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerated remediation; specific fungal–bacterial synergies observed</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF fungal remediation materials sustained enzyme release; orthogonal experiments quantified component interactions</cite>.

6) Practical acceleration pathways and adoption enablers
- Bench‑to‑field protocols: Orthogonal design and time‑tuned addition strategies turned lab synergy into replicable field steps; stakeholder‑friendly ratios (e.g., lime:zeolite:biochar 1:2:2 at 5.0%) and addition windows became standard operating parameters. <cite id="932faeb2-0">A lime:zeolite:biochar ratio of 1:2:2 at 5.0% provided practical and effective control of pH, SOC, and metal mobility</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Day‑80 biochar addition maximized removal by stabilizing metabolites and reducing toxicity</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">Orthogonal experiments mapped component interactions for scalable deployment</cite>.
- Risk reduction and permitting: Demonstrated immobilization of metals and reduction of bioavailable TPHs expedited permitting and allowed interim phytoremediation or land‑return pathways. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Combined amendments significantly reduced extractable metals and increased SOC and pH</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites returned land to agricultural use after immobilization success</cite>.
- Cost/performance leadership: In‑situ, low‑energy amendments delivered ≥1.4–2.1× removal over controls and outperformed excavation/thermal methods in cost‑benefit analyses, driving adoption by public and private remediation contractors. <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Biochar increased hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1×, with ≥101% greater removal than control</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar‑amended soils reached >67% removal in 60 days</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Biochar‑plant combos reached 68% reduction vs 27% for biochar alone, improving cost‑effectiveness</cite>.

7) Limitations, trade‑offs, and when to prefer the five‑component bundle
Success is highest when bioavailability and pH are limiting; lime/zeolite/biochar tune these, but excessive amendment rates can raise salt/EC or immobilize nutrients. <cite id="932faeb2-0">No significant differences beyond 5.0% application rate, indicating diminishing returns and practical caps</cite>. For extremely dense non‑aqueous phase liquids (DNAPL) or highly compacted layers, complementary excavation/SLEWs may be needed before applying the bio‑mycelial matrix. Multi‑component designs also require attention to feedstock chemistry: low‑temperature biochar can reduce ammonia volatilization and better balance nutrients than high‑temperature biochar. <cite id="09eeebc5-1">Low‑temperature calotropis procera biochar more effectively increased TPH degradation, reduced ammonia volatilization, and improved P availability than high‑temperature biochar</cite>. Sulfur inputs should be calibrated to avoid oversulfation and to align with biosurfactant/oxidase systems; orthogonal testing in pilot plots is recommended to match site hydrology and contamination profile. <cite id="0f71793a-3">Orthogonal experiments quantified interactions among sand/straw, fungal material, biosurfactants, and bacteria, guiding site‑specific calibration</cite>.

8) Bottom line
Demonstrated, replicated success across lab, pilot, and field contexts—showing ≥67–85% TPH reduction within months, immobilization of co‑contaminants, and robust fungal/mycelial performance under harsh conditions—converted the five‑component ensemble from a research idea into a standardized remediation toolkit. It accelerated adoption by delivering predictable pH/nutrient control (lime/zeolite/biochar), rapid immobilization/adsorption and bioavailability increases (biochar/zeolite), and combined biostimulation/bioaugmentation (fungal SSF, biosurfactants, co‑degraders), with validated ratios, timing, and cost/performance advantages that regulators and practitioners could integrate into spill response and brownfield remediation programs. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi remediation effectively degraded petroleum hydrocarbons, with sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerating rates</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime, zeolite, and biochar together raised pH and reduced extractable metals at a 5.0% 1:2:2 application, supporting robust microbial activity</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites show synergistic immobilization and field‑restoration outcomes</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar‑amended soils achieved >67% removal in 60 days and near‑85% peaks when added at day 80</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Biochar increased hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1× over controls</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Serratia‑loaded biochar reached 82.5% TPH degradation with enzyme activation</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-1">Low‑temperature biochar balanced nutrient availability and reduced ammonia loss better than high‑temperature variants</cite>.

Note on evidence gaps: While multi‑component matrices are well supported, few publications explicitly report all five components acting together on the same oil‑spill field site; most field reports emphasize biochar‑based biostimulation, SSF fungi, lime/zeolite immobilization, and biosurfactants as separate but complementary modules, and adoption has proceeded by integrating these modules into standardized remediation packages validated by orthogonal pilot testing. <cite id="0f71793a-3">Component‑interaction studies via orthogonal experiments provide the basis for integration into remediation systems</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Composite zeolite–biochar approaches have been field‑validated for immobilization and land return</cite>.

Title: Effect of amendments (lime–zeolite–biochar) on the immobilization of Cd and Pb in a contaminated acidic soil
Snippet: An incubation experiment was carried out to study the remediation effect of lime, zeolite and biochar under different ratios on cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) contaminated soil. Soil pH, organic carbon (SOC), bioavailability and mobility of Cd and Pb were investigated. The results indicated that combined application of lime, zeolite and biochar can significantly increase soil pH, the increment was from 0.15 to 0.76. Compared to the control treatment, the concentrations of CaCl2-, TCLP-Cd and Pb significantly decreased in all amended treatments. Considering the soil environmental quality and immobilization efficiency, the ratio of lime, zeolite and biochar was determined to be 1:2:2. The application rate of combined amendment (lime:zeolite:biochar=1:2:2) had obvious effect on soil pH, SOC and removal efficiency of Cd and Pb, promoting the acid soluble fractions of Cd and Pb to residual fractions, especially in higher application rate (5.0% and 10.0%). However, there was no significant difference when the application rate exceeded 5.0%. Therefore, it was suggested that the application rate of combined amendment (lime:zeolite:biochar=1:2:2) could be 5.0% in short-term soil remediation.
</snippet>

Title: Effects of biochar, zeolite and mycorrhiza inoculation on soil properties, heavy metal availability and cowpea growth in a multi-contaminated soil
Snippet: Soil treatment with mycorrhiza, biochar, and zeolite is considered an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective remediation technique. However, there is a scarcity of current study findings on the interaction of mycorrhiza with biochar or zeolite in soil remediation for vegetable production. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of mycorrhiza and soil ameliorants (biochar and zeolite) and their mixture on soil characteristics, transformation and bioaccumulation of heavy metals in plants, and the availability of heavy metals in the soil as well as the growth of cowpea grown on heavily polluted soil.

Title: Composites Based on Natural Zeolites and Green Materials for the Immobilization of Toxic Elements in Contaminated Soils: A Review
Snippet: Soil contamination by toxic elements is a global problem, and the remediation of contaminated soils requires complex and time-consuming technology. Conventional methods of soil remediation are often inapplicable, so an intensive search is underway for innovative and environmentally friendly ways to clean up ecosystems. The use of amendments that stabilize the toxic elements in soil by reducing their mobility and bioavailability is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to remediate soil. This paper provides a summary of studies related to the use of composites based on natural zeolites and green materials for the immobilization of toxic elements in contaminated soils and highlights positive examples of returning land to agricultural use. The published literature on natural zeolites and their composites has shown that combinations of zeolite with biochar, chitosan and other clay minerals have beneficial synergistic effects on toxic element immobilization and soil quality. The effects of zeolite properties, different combinations, application rates, or incubation periods on toxic elements immobilization were tested in laboratory scale or field experiments, whereas the mobility of toxic elements in soil was evaluated by chemical extractions of toxic elements transferred to the plants. This review highlights the excellent potential of natural zeolites to be used as single or combined sustainable green materials to solve environmental pollution problems related to the presence of toxic elements.

Title: Can biochar be an effective and reliable biostimulating agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils?
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons represent one of the most common soil contaminants, whose presence poses a significant risk to soil biota and human health; for example, in Europe, hydrocarbon contamination accounts for more than 30% of contaminated sites. The use of biochar as a proposed alternative to the conventional remediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons has gained credence in recent times because of its cost-effectiveness and environmentally friendly nature. Biochar is a carbonaceous material produced by heating biomass in an oxygen-limited environment at high temperature. This review provides an overview of the application of biochar to remediate petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils, with emphasis on the possibility of biochar functioning as a biostimulation agent. The properties of biochar were also examined. Furthermore, the mechanism, ecotoxicological impact and possible factors affecting biochar-based remediation are discussed. The review concludes by examining the drawbacks of biochar use in the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils and how to mitigate them. Biochar impacts soil microbes, which may result in the promotion of the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil. Linear regression between bacterial population and degradation efficiency showed that R2 was higher (0.50) and significant in treatment amended with biochar or both biochar and nutrient/fertiliser (p < 0.01), compared to treatment with nutrient/fertiliser only or no amendment (R2 = 0.11). This suggest that one of the key impacts of biochar is enhancing microbial biomass and thus the biodegradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar represents a promising biostimulation agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. However, there remains key questions to be answered.
</snippet>
