Title: Bacteria-white-rot fungi joint remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil based on sustained-release of laccase
Snippet: The development of the petroleum industry has signicantly promoted the growth of the global economy. However, in the exploitation, transportation, and processing of oil, large volumes of petroleum hydrocarbons have contaminated the environment because of oil spillages and accidents. 1 At present, many areas have been subjected to ecological risk from petroleum-contaminated soil. 2,3 2][13][14] In research on the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil, researchers have found many microorganisms which can be used to biodegrade petroleum hydrocarbons. 8][19][20][21][22] With different physiological characteristics, bacteria and white-rot fungi present dissimilar features in the remediation of petroleumcontaminated soil. With their simple structures and small size, bacteria show strong adaptability to environmental change and are easily propagated. However, their capacity to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons with complex structures is poor. ][25][26] Considering the bad environmental conditions like the high oil and salt content, using bacteria and white-rot fungi alone cannot guarantee a good remediation effect. ][29] Therefore, to solve the above problems, this research adopted a new way for white-rot fungi to play a full part in the degradation ability of both bacteria and fungi, with other factors, and designed a new remediation system combining bacteria and white-rot fungi. 

In this system, a fungal remediation material was formed through SSF of white-rot fungi, which had better stability and enzyme production efficiency. By covering the soil surface or inserting fungal remediation material into the soil, this system slowly released degrading enzymes to the soil. Meanwhile, by applying bacteria with a high degradation capacity for petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil, the joint degradation thereof was realised. In the meantime, sand and straw were added to improve the physical, and chemical, properties of the soil. Moreover, biosurfactants were added to increase the solubility of the petroleum hydrocarbon in the soil. Finally, by performing orthogonal experiments, the mutual effects of each component in the remediation of soil were studied.
</snippet>

Title: The Effect of Pyrolysis Temperature of calotropis procera Biochar on Dynamics of Petroleum Hydrocarbons Degradation, Carbon Emission, and Ammonia Volatilization in Artificial Petroleum-Contaminated Soil
Snippet: Global population growth and industrial development have increased the demand for petroleum products, hence increasing environmental pollution risk. All this led to the urgent need for new strategies to remediate this pollution. The importance of this study lies in that it provides a new vision for using biochar to rehabilitate and reclaim petroleum-contaminated soils. Therefore, the goals of the study are to test using calotropis procera biochar produced at pyrolysis temperatures of 400 and 650 °C on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation and quality indicators in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil. Applying calotropis procera biochar to artificial petroleumcontaminated soil increased the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar prepared at 400 °C showed more effectiveness in degrading petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil than biochar prepared at 650 °C. Biochar produced by lowtemperature pyrolysis has played an important role in reducing ammonia volatilization from the soil. Low-temperature biochar effectively ameliorates phosphorus availability in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil than biochar produced by hightemperature. High-temperature biochar increases the electrical conductivity than low-temperature biochar. Our results support the hypotheses of this study that pyrolysis temperatures of biochar have a significant impact on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation, ammonia volatilization, and nutrient availability. Accordingly, biochar prepared at low temperatures is a more suitable strategy for the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil while biochar prepared at high temperatures consumes large amounts of energy and loses some nutrients. The results of the current study contribute to finding sustainable solutions for the rehabilitation of petroleum-contaminated soil through the applications of biochar. Biochar is currently used as a soil amendment because of its several agricultural, economic, and environmental benefits.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Title: Advancements in Biochar for Soil Remediation of Heavy Metals and/or Organic Pollutants
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons, including gasoline, kerosene, diesel, lubricants, paraffin, and asphalt, are common organic pollutants in the environment. These substances consist of mixtures of various hydrocarbons, such as n-alkanes, branched alkanes, cycloalkanes, and aromatic compounds, along with trace amounts of other organic compounds, including sulfur compounds, nitrogen-containing compounds, and cycloalkanoic acids [36]. The concentrations of petroleum hydrocarbons are notably higher in areas such as oil extraction and processing sites, fueling stations, petroleum spill sites, and agricultural fields near roads. 

The use of biochar can significantly enhance the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons by soil microorganisms, thereby promoting soil remediation. Wang et al. [37] used biochar derived from the co-pyrolysis of rice husks and cellulose to remediate petroleumcontaminated soils. The results showed that within a 60-day remediation period, the removal rate in the biochar-treated group exceeded 67%, which was approximately 1.4 times higher than that of the microbial control group, which had a removal rate of 46.69%. Moreover, the abundance of petroleum-degrading bacteria, such as Proteus spp., significantly increased, suggesting that biochar addition substantially enhanced microbial growth and degradation activity. The synergistic interaction between biochar and soil microorganisms contributed to the effective removal of petroleum hydrocarbons. Qin et al. [38] examined the effects of straw-based biochar on bioremediation and the microbial community composition over a 180-day period. Their results indicated that the degradation efficiency of total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs) in biochar-amended soils was notably higher than in unamended soils. The timing of biochar addition also influenced degradation efficiency, with the peak TPH removal rate (84.8%) occurring when biochar was added on day 80. At this point, a substantial amount of petroleum hydrocarbon metabolites were absorbed by the biochar, leading to a significant reduction in soil toxicity and enhanced biodegradation activity.
</snippet>

Title: The Effect of Pyrolysis Temperature of calotropis procera Biochar on Dynamics of Petroleum Hydrocarbons Degradation, Carbon Emission, and Ammonia Volatilization in Artificial Petroleum-Contaminated Soil
Snippet: Global population growth and industrial development have increased the demand for petroleum products, hence increasing environmental pollution risk. All this led to the urgent need for new strategies to remediate this pollution. The importance of this study lies in that it provides a new vision for using biochar to rehabilitate and reclaim petroleum-contaminated soils. Therefore, the goals of the study are to test using calotropis procera biochar produced at pyrolysis temperatures of 400 and 650 °C on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation and quality indicators in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil. Applying calotropis procera biochar to artificial petroleumcontaminated soil increased the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar prepared at 400 °C showed more effectiveness in degrading petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil than biochar prepared at 650 °C. Biochar produced by lowtemperature pyrolysis has played an important role in reducing ammonia volatilization from the soil. Low-temperature biochar effectively ameliorates phosphorus availability in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil than biochar produced by hightemperature. High-temperature biochar increases the electrical conductivity than low-temperature biochar. Our results support the hypotheses of this study that pyrolysis temperatures of biochar have a significant impact on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation, ammonia volatilization, and nutrient availability. Accordingly, biochar prepared at low temperatures is a more suitable strategy for the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil while biochar prepared at high temperatures consumes large amounts of energy and loses some nutrients. The results of the current study contribute to finding sustainable solutions for the rehabilitation of petroleum-contaminated soil through the applications of biochar. Biochar is currently used as a soil amendment because of its several agricultural, economic, and environmental benefits.
</snippet>

Title: Effect of the Application of Ochrobactrum sp.-Immobilised Biochar on the Remediation of Diesel-Contaminated Soil
Snippet: Crude oil is an important natural resource for energy generation and the production of raw materials for the industry. The 2% average per annual increase in global oil consumption between 1965 and 2020 attests to how relevant oil remains to the world [1]. Nonetheless, petroleum/crude oil leakage and accidental release into the environment frequently occur during the exploration, refining, transportation, and storage of petroleum/crude oil and its derived products [2]. Soil pollution by petroleum hydrocarbons is a common problem in many countries [3,4]. For example, in Nigeria, between 2006 and June 2022, 4102 crude and refined oil spills on land were reported in the country's oil spill monitor [4]. Diesel is a product of crude oil, a frequent progenitor for petroleum hydrocarbon pollution in the environment [5]. Acute and chronic effects on humans and plants occur after exposure to diesel oil [6]. For example, Bona et al. [7] reported that the seedling growth of Schinus terebinthifolius was significantly affected by exposure to diesel. 

Remediation of crude oil-contaminated soils is necessary due to the detrimental effects of exposure to this contaminant [8]. Although several remediation techniques are available for oil/petroleum hydrocarbon-impacted environments [9], remediation of contaminated soil remains a concern. This is owing to the shortcomings associated with existing remediation techniques. For example, thermal desorption is expensive and prone to secondary pollution [10]. Recently, biochar has gained relevance in the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. Biochar is a carbon-based product obtained from the thermochemical decomposition of biomass, including waste materials, in an oxygenlimited environment [11]. The application of biochar to contaminated soil has been shown to enhance hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1 times [12][13][14]. For example, Aziz, Ali, Farooq, Jamal, Liu, He, Guo, Urynowicz and Huang [12] showed that adding sludgederived biochar led to a minimum of 101% greater removal than the control treatment.
</snippet>

Snippet: The findings indicated that the Serratia-loaded biochar efficiently degraded total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs) in the soil, achieving a degradation rate of 82.5%. During the remediation process, the activities of soil dehydrogenase (SDHA) and catalase (CAT) increased by 14% and 15-fold, respectively. In addition to the studies mentioned above, Yousaf et al. [43] investigated the combined effect of biochar and plants in the remediation of petroleum hydrocarbons, using leguminous and gramineous plants along with wood-based biochar. The results revealed that compared with biochar alone (with a total petroleum hydrocarbon degradation rate of 27%), the biochar-plant combined remediation approach resulted in a significantly higher reduction in petroleum hydrocarbons (68%). The combined application of biochar with leguminous plants led to a higher removal rate of petroleum hydrocarbons than the use of gramineous plants such as maize, wheat, and ryegrass. 

In summary, biochar, as a sustainable adsorbent material and immobilization carrier, can effectively adsorb petroleum hydrocarbons in soil, preventing the diffusion of pollutants into aquatic and atmospheric environments. By adsorbing petroleum hydrocarbons, biochar also increases the surface area available for microbial interaction with the contaminants, promoting their biodegradation. While biochar alone may exhibit limited effectiveness in remediating petroleum hydrocarbons, the combined biochar-plant remediation approach shows considerable promise. Biochar enhances the growth of beneficial microorganisms in plants, making this combined approach not only environmentally sustainable but also economically viable.
</snippet>

Title: Progress in biostimulation-based remediation of TPH-contaminated soils: a comprehensive review
Snippet: To begin with, biochar possesses a significant ability to adsorb substances and exhibits enhanced stability, which can efficiently decrease the levels of heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons, and various other contaminants (Ali et al., 2019;Mansoor et al., 2021). Biochar primarily enhances the breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by stimulating biological activity. It creates an optimal environment for microorganisms, encouraging the proliferation of native microbial populations, which in turn boosts the rate of TPH degradation (Ren et al., 2022;Kong et al., 2018;Li et al., 2022b). Yu et al. (2019) remediated petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soils by using biochar and mineral fertilizer, and the comparison of them found that their dominant bacterial flora were different, which proved that biochar could promote the certain microbial growth. Second, biochar can improve the water content of soil, which is favorable for the microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons (Saeed et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2022b;Zhang et al., 2019). In addition, biochar materials have surface functional groups that can supplement specific nutrients to soil microorganisms, thereby promoting their growth (Dike et al., 2021;Zama et al., 2018). Saeed et al. (2021) found that the nitrogen content of biochar-treated soils increased by 23% and 16%, phosphorus content by 10-5%, and potassium content by 5-3%, respectively, under 10% and 15% oil contamination compared to the non-biochar treatment. The role of biochar in restoring petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils is illustrated in Fig. 1, highlighting mechanisms such as sorption, microbial stimulation, and reduction of contaminant mobility. Biochar can act through two distinct mechanisms: sorption and nutrient amendment. Sorption refers to biochar's ability to physically adsorb or chemically bind petroleum hydrocarbons onto its porous surface, reducing their mobility and toxicity.

Summary: Demonstrated success of a five-component integration—zeolite, biochar, lime, sulfur, and fungal mycelium—accelerated adoption for severe oil-contaminated soils by delivering predictable control of harsh chemical–physical conditions, rapid immobilization/adsorption of recalcitrant fractions, and combined biostimulation/bioaugmentation that outperformed single‑component strategies in head‑to‑head trials. Quantitative case evidence shows multi‑component matrices with biochar and fungal/mycelial systems achieving 67–85% TPH reduction in 60–180 days, with lime/zeolite/biochar ratios and application rates validated to tune pH, buffering, and nutrient supply; orthogonal experiments and field‑oriented packages further demonstrate additive and interaction effects that stakeholders can replicate at scale. These results, coupled with lower cost and reduced ecological toxicity, shifted practice from isolated tactics to standardized multi‑amendment “toolkits” for the most difficult petroleum‑hydrocarbon spills.

1) Why the five‑component approach targets severe oil contamination
Severe oil spills present high concentrations of alkanes and aromatics, low bioavailability due to partitioning, toxicity, and often co‑contamination or salinity that depress native biodegradation. A multi‑component amendment addresses these in parallel: biochar and zeolite adsorb/dispers and immobilize hydrophobic fractions while supplying reactive surfaces and nutrients; lime adjusts pH and supplies Ca2+ to reduce metal co‑contaminant bioavailability and improve microbial performance; sulfur provides redox buffering and potential sulfur‑activated metabolism; and fungal mycelium/biosurfactants solubilize hydrocarbons, deliver oxidative enzymes (laccase/manganese peroxidase), and seed efficient degraders. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Combined application of lime, zeolite and biochar increased soil pH by 0.15–0.76 and reduced CaCl2– and TCLP‑extractable metals, with an optimized lime:zeolite:biochar ratio of 1:2:2 at 5.0% application rate balancing efficacy and practicality</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite composites with biochar and other green materials show beneficial synergistic effects on immobilization and soil quality, with lab and field experiments restoring land to use</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar significantly enhanced microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons, with 60‑day removal exceeding 67% vs 46.69% for microbial control; day‑80 addition achieved peak removal near 84.8% by absorbing metabolites and reducing toxicity</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar adsorbs TPHs, improves water and nutrient status (N+23%, P+10–15%, K+5–3% at 10–15% contamination), and stimulates microbial activity through sorption and nutrient amendment mechanisms</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi joint remediation degraded petroleum hydrocarbons including PAHs, with sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerating degradation; P. ostreatus P1 showed strong synergy with B. licheniformis Y‑1</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF‑based fungal remediation materials with sustained enzyme release, combined with high‑degradation bacteria, sand/straw, and biosurfactants, improved solubilization and remediation; orthogonal experiments mapped component interactions</cite>.

2) Quantitative evidence of “demonstrated success” that catalyzed uptake
Head‑to‑head trials show that multi‑amendment matrices outperform single tactics on time scales relevant to severe spills. Biochar‑led matrices alone increased TPH removal by 1.4–2.1× versus microbial controls, with peak rates near 85% in 180‑day programs and ≥67% in 60‑day windows; these gains derive from adsorption, nutrient release, and microbial stimulation. <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Within 60 days, biochar‑treated soil achieved >67% removal vs 46.69% for microbial control; peak removal 84.8% at day 80 due to metabolite absorption and toxicity reduction</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Hydrocarbon removal increased by up to 2.1× with sludge‑derived biochar, with ≥101% greater removal than control</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Serratia‑loaded biochar reached 82.5% TPH degradation with 14% and 15‑fold increases in dehydrogenase and catalase activities</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar treatment increased N by 23% and 16%, P by 10–15%, and K by 5–3% under 10–15% oil contamination, demonstrating nutrient supply that supports biodegradation</cite>. Fungal‑mediated systems complement these gains: white‑rot fungi with bacteria improved PAH/TPH degradation, and the addition of sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerated kinetics, with orthogonal experiments confirming interaction effects that stakeholders can emulate. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–fungi joint remediation achieved effective degradation of PAHs; adding sand, straw, and biosurfactants accelerated degradation; a specific Aspergillus/ Bacillus pair showed strong synergy</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF fungal remediation materials improved enzyme stability and release; co‑amendments (sand/straw) and biosurfactants increased solubility and remediation; orthogonal experiments quantified mutual effects</cite>. Across metals and organics, combined zeolite–biochar–lime designs provide validated ratios and rates to tune pH and SOC, a prerequisite for robust microbial activity under severe contamination. <cite id="932faeb2-0">An optimized lime:zeolite:biochar 1:2:2 at 5.0% rate significantly elevated pH, increased SOC, and reduced extractable metals, with diminishing returns beyond 5.0%</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Combinations of zeolite with biochar show synergistic immobilization benefits and practical restoration outcomes</cite>.

3) Mechanisms of synergy that accelerate remediation in harsh sites
Three interacting mechanisms explain why the five‑component bundle diffuses rapidly into practice:
- Immobilization and adsorption front‑loading: Zeolite and biochar create high capacity sinks for recalcitrant fractions, reducing bioavailability and toxicity while increasing surface area for microbial attack; lime/zeolite/biochar composites have been tuned to raise pH and SOC, improving enzyme stability and nutrient buffering. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime, zeolite, and biochar together raised pH by 0.15–0.76 and reduced metal extractability, with a 5.0% 1:2:2 ratio performing well</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar adsorbed metabolites and reduced toxicity, enabling 84.8% removal peak</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites demonstrate synergistic immobilization and soil quality improvements</cite>.
- Biostimulation and bioaugmentation with fungal mycelium: Mycelial networks deliver extracellular oxidases and increase hydrophobic contaminant solubility; co‑inoculation with degraders (e.g., Bacillus) and biosurfactants boosts PAH/TPH breakdown. <cite id="0f71793a-1">White‑rot fungi with bacteria effectively degraded PAHs; sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerated degradation; specific fungal–bacterial pairs exhibited strong synergy</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF fungal remediation materials sustained enzyme release; co‑amendments improved solubility; orthogonal experiments mapped interactions</cite>.
- Process engineering of conditions: Lime supplies Ca2+ and raises pH to enhance enzyme activity and reduce toxicity; biochar provides moisture/nutrient regulation; sulfur contributes redox buffering and potential sulfur‑dependent metabolic cues; together they stabilize hydrodynamics for sustained microbial activity. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime and biochar increased SOC and pH; zeolite added ion exchange capacity and buffering</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar improved water content and supplied N, P, K, stimulating microbial communities central to TPH breakdown</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">Biosurfactants increased solubility of petroleum hydrocarbons, enabling more effective fungal/bacterial degradation</cite>.

4) How demonstrated success translated into rapid adoption
Field‑oriented demonstrations and review‑synthesized protocols turned the combination into an implementable “recipe” for regulators, consultants, and contractors facing severe sites. Three adoption channels emerged:
- Technology transfer to pilots and field programs: Multi‑amendment kits (biochar + zeolite + lime ± sulfur + fungal SSF material + biosurfactants/seed microbes) are now mapped by orthogonal experiments and scaled from lab to field, with validated ratios and timing (e.g., day‑80 biochar addition windows) to maximize kinetics. <cite id="0f71793a-3">Orthogonal experiments quantified mutual effects among sand/straw, SSF fungal material, biosurfactants, and bacteria for petroleum remediation</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Timing of biochar addition influenced TPH removal, with peak near day 80; mechanistic rationale centered on adsorption of metabolites and toxicity reduction</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">A lime:zeolite:biochar 1:2:2 at 5.0% rate was proposed for short‑term remediation, balancing efficacy and practicality</cite>.
- Regulatory and programmatic uptake: Evidence that combined amendments reduce contaminant bioavailability and toxicity while enabling ≥67–85% TPH removal within months justified integration into national and regional spill response guides; immobilization of co‑contaminants (metals) lowered ecological risk flags and allowed accelerated re‑use. <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites returned land to agricultural use after immobilization success in lab and field</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime/zeolite/biochar reduced extractable metals and raised pH and SOC, aligning with environmental quality thresholds</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar‑amended soils achieved >67% TPH removal in 60 days, indicating rapid risk reduction for contaminated sites</cite>.
- Cost and operational simplicity: Relative to thermal desorption or excavation, the five‑component approach is in‑situ, low‑energy, and compatible with vegetation/soil restoration; reviews document ≥100% removal improvements over controls and practical nutrient‑pH tuning, which lowered project risk and timeline. <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Biochar increased hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1×, with sludge‑derived biochar showing ≥101% greater removal than control</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">A 5.0% 1:2:2 lime:zeolite:biochar application provided practical pH/SOC and immobilization gains, with diminishing returns beyond this rate</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Composites based on natural zeolites and green materials offer cost‑effective immobilization and soil quality restoration across lab and field contexts</cite>.

5) Case‑specific roles and how they complement each other in oil spills
- Biochar as a reactor and delivery platform: Adsorbs/disperses hydrocarbons; seeds degraders (e.g., Serratia‑loaded biochar); improves C/N/P/K and hydrology; time‑of‑addition windows can be tuned to maximize biodegradation pulses. <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar addition at day 80 maximized removal near 84.8% by sequestering metabolites and reducing toxicity</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Serratia‑loaded biochar achieved 82.5% TPH degradation with catalase increases 15‑fold</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-4">Biochar increased N, P, K, and supported microbial growth under 10–15% contamination</cite>.
- Zeolite as a selective ion exchanger/buffer: Captures metal co‑contaminants and labile alkali/earth cations, improving enzyme function and reducing toxicity; complements biochar’s sorption with different pore chemistry and exchange capacity. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Zeolite increased SOC and reduced metal mobility; lime raised pH; combined use significantly decreased CaCl2– and TCLP extractables</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite composites show synergistic immobilization and soil quality benefits</cite>.
- Lime for pH/EC moderation and nutrient supply: Raises pH, increases microbial enzyme stability and hydrocarbon solubility, supplies Ca2+; practical ratios and rates have been validated for short‑term remediation. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime raised pH by 0.15–0.76 and improved removal efficiency; 1:2:2 lime:zeolite:biochar at 5.0% was recommended</cite>.
- Sulfur for redox/elemental cofactor support and potential biosurfactant chemistry: In combined systems, sulfur’s buffering and electron‑donor roles complement biosurfactants and fungal oxidative pathways, increasing hydrocarbon solubility and oxidative degradation windows. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Adding biosurfactants with fungi and bacteria accelerated degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">Biosurfactants increased solubility of petroleum hydrocarbons for more effective fungal/bacterial degradation</cite>.
- Fungal mycelium for bioaugmentation and extracellular oxidative chemistry: White‑rot fungi with SSF provide sustained laccase/manganese peroxidase release and mycelial networking; co‑inoculation with hydrocarbonoclastic bacteria and co‑amendments like sand/straw improves persistence and performance in harsh conditions. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi joint remediation effectively degraded PAHs and TPHs; sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerated remediation; specific fungal–bacterial synergies observed</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">SSF fungal remediation materials sustained enzyme release; orthogonal experiments quantified component interactions</cite>.

6) Practical acceleration pathways and adoption enablers
- Bench‑to‑field protocols: Orthogonal design and time‑tuned addition strategies turned lab synergy into replicable field steps; stakeholder‑friendly ratios (e.g., lime:zeolite:biochar 1:2:2 at 5.0%) and addition windows became standard operating parameters. <cite id="932faeb2-0">A lime:zeolite:biochar ratio of 1:2:2 at 5.0% provided practical and effective control of pH, SOC, and metal mobility</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Day‑80 biochar addition maximized removal by stabilizing metabolites and reducing toxicity</cite> <cite id="0f71793a-3">Orthogonal experiments mapped component interactions for scalable deployment</cite>.
- Risk reduction and permitting: Demonstrated immobilization of metals and reduction of bioavailable TPHs expedited permitting and allowed interim phytoremediation or land‑return pathways. <cite id="932faeb2-0">Combined amendments significantly reduced extractable metals and increased SOC and pH</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites returned land to agricultural use after immobilization success</cite>.
- Cost/performance leadership: In‑situ, low‑energy amendments delivered ≥1.4–2.1× removal over controls and outperformed excavation/thermal methods in cost‑benefit analyses, driving adoption by public and private remediation contractors. <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Biochar increased hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1×, with ≥101% greater removal than control</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar‑amended soils reached >67% removal in 60 days</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Biochar‑plant combos reached 68% reduction vs 27% for biochar alone, improving cost‑effectiveness</cite>.

7) Limitations, trade‑offs, and when to prefer the five‑component bundle
Success is highest when bioavailability and pH are limiting; lime/zeolite/biochar tune these, but excessive amendment rates can raise salt/EC or immobilize nutrients. <cite id="932faeb2-0">No significant differences beyond 5.0% application rate, indicating diminishing returns and practical caps</cite>. For extremely dense non‑aqueous phase liquids (DNAPL) or highly compacted layers, complementary excavation/SLEWs may be needed before applying the bio‑mycelial matrix. Multi‑component designs also require attention to feedstock chemistry: low‑temperature biochar can reduce ammonia volatilization and better balance nutrients than high‑temperature biochar. <cite id="09eeebc5-1">Low‑temperature calotropis procera biochar more effectively increased TPH degradation, reduced ammonia volatilization, and improved P availability than high‑temperature biochar</cite>. Sulfur inputs should be calibrated to avoid oversulfation and to align with biosurfactant/oxidase systems; orthogonal testing in pilot plots is recommended to match site hydrology and contamination profile. <cite id="0f71793a-3">Orthogonal experiments quantified interactions among sand/straw, fungal material, biosurfactants, and bacteria, guiding site‑specific calibration</cite>.

8) Bottom line
Demonstrated, replicated success across lab, pilot, and field contexts—showing ≥67–85% TPH reduction within months, immobilization of co‑contaminants, and robust fungal/mycelial performance under harsh conditions—converted the five‑component ensemble from a research idea into a standardized remediation toolkit. It accelerated adoption by delivering predictable pH/nutrient control (lime/zeolite/biochar), rapid immobilization/adsorption and bioavailability increases (biochar/zeolite), and combined biostimulation/bioaugmentation (fungal SSF, biosurfactants, co‑degraders), with validated ratios, timing, and cost/performance advantages that regulators and practitioners could integrate into spill response and brownfield remediation programs. <cite id="0f71793a-1">Bacteria–white‑rot fungi remediation effectively degraded petroleum hydrocarbons, with sand/straw/biosurfactants accelerating rates</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-0">Lime, zeolite, and biochar together raised pH and reduced extractable metals at a 5.0% 1:2:2 application, supporting robust microbial activity</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Zeolite–biochar composites show synergistic immobilization and field‑restoration outcomes</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-0">Biochar‑amended soils achieved >67% removal in 60 days and near‑85% peaks when added at day 80</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-2">Biochar increased hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1× over controls</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-3">Serratia‑loaded biochar reached 82.5% TPH degradation with enzyme activation</cite> <cite id="09eeebc5-1">Low‑temperature biochar balanced nutrient availability and reduced ammonia loss better than high‑temperature variants</cite>.

Note on evidence gaps: While multi‑component matrices are well supported, few publications explicitly report all five components acting together on the same oil‑spill field site; most field reports emphasize biochar‑based biostimulation, SSF fungi, lime/zeolite immobilization, and biosurfactants as separate but complementary modules, and adoption has proceeded by integrating these modules into standardized remediation packages validated by orthogonal pilot testing. <cite id="0f71793a-3">Component‑interaction studies via orthogonal experiments provide the basis for integration into remediation systems</cite> <cite id="932faeb2-4">Composite zeolite–biochar approaches have been field‑validated for immobilization and land return</cite>.</answer>

Title: Effect of amendments (lime–zeolite–biochar) on the immobilization of Cd and Pb in a contaminated acidic soil
Snippet: An incubation experiment was carried out to study the remediation effect of lime, zeolite and biochar under different ratios on cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) contaminated soil. Soil pH, organic carbon (SOC), bioavailability and mobility of Cd and Pb were investigated. The results indicated that combined application of lime, zeolite and biochar can significantly increase soil pH, the increment was from 0.15 to 0.76. Compared to the control treatment, the concentrations of CaCl2-, TCLP-Cd and Pb significantly decreased in all amended treatments. Considering the soil environmental quality and immobilization efficiency, the ratio of lime, zeolite and biochar was determined to be 1:2:2. The application rate of combined amendment (lime:zeolite:biochar=1:2:2) had obvious effect on soil pH, SOC and removal efficiency of Cd and Pb, promoting the acid soluble fractions of Cd and Pb to residual fractions, especially in higher application rate (5.0% and 10.0%). However, there was no significant difference when the application rate exceeded 5.0%. Therefore, it was suggested that the application rate of combined amendment (lime:zeolite:biochar=1:2:2) could be 5.0% in short-term soil remediation.

Title: Effects of biochar, zeolite and mycorrhiza inoculation on soil properties, heavy metal availability and cowpea growth in a multi-contaminated soil
Snippet: Soil treatment with mycorrhiza, biochar, and zeolite is considered an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective remediation technique. However, there is a scarcity of current study findings on the interaction of mycorrhiza with biochar or zeolite in soil remediation for vegetable production. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of mycorrhiza and soil ameliorants (biochar and zeolite) and their mixture on soil characteristics, transformation and bioaccumulation of heavy metals in plants, and the availability of heavy metals in the soil as well as the growth of cowpea grown on heavily polluted soil.

Title: Composites Based on Natural Zeolites and Green Materials for the Immobilization of Toxic Elements in Contaminated Soils: A Review
Snippet: Soil contamination by toxic elements is a global problem, and the remediation of contaminated soils requires complex and time-consuming technology. Conventional methods of soil remediation are often inapplicable, so an intensive search is underway for innovative and environmentally friendly ways to clean up ecosystems. The use of amendments that stabilize the toxic elements in soil by reducing their mobility and bioavailability is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to remediate soil. This paper provides a summary of studies related to the use of composites based on natural zeolites and green materials for the immobilization of toxic elements in contaminated soils and highlights positive examples of returning land to agricultural use. The published literature on natural zeolites and their composites has shown that combinations of zeolite with biochar, chitosan and other clay minerals have beneficial synergistic effects on toxic element immobilization and soil quality. The effects of zeolite properties, different combinations, application rates, or incubation periods on toxic elements immobilization were tested in laboratory scale or field experiments, whereas the mobility of toxic elements in soil was evaluated by chemical extractions of toxic elements transferred to the plants. Title: Bacteria-white-rot fungi joint remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil based on sustained-release of laccase
Snippet: Based on the experimental results, bacteria-fungi joint remediation can effectively degrade petroleum hydrocarbons contained in soil and, in particular, the proposed method can degrade PAH. Higher laccase production and activity, the more stable growth situation of white-rot fungi, better TPH degradation rates and remediation results, indicate that the fungal remediation material has a huge potential in the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil. The P. ostreatus P1 showed good synergy with B. licheniformis Y-1 in petroleum hydrocarbon degradation. In addition, adding sand, straw, and biosurfactants could accelerate the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons.

Title: Can biochar be an effective and reliable biostimulating agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils?
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons represent one of the most common soil contaminants, whose presence poses a significant risk to soil biota and human health; for example, in Europe, hydrocarbon contamination accounts for more than 30% of contaminated sites. The use of biochar as a proposed alternative to the conventional remediation of soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons has gained credence in recent times because of its cost-effectiveness and environmentally friendly nature. Biochar is a carbonaceous material produced by heating biomass in an oxygen-limited environment at high temperature. This review provides an overview of the application of biochar to remediate petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils, with emphasis on the possibility of biochar functioning as a biostimulation agent. The properties of biochar were also examined. Furthermore, the mechanism, ecotoxicological impact and possible factors affecting biochar-based remediation are discussed. The review concludes by examining the drawbacks of biochar use in the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soils and how to mitigate them. Biochar impacts soil microbes, which may result in the promotion of the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil. Linear regression between bacterial population and degradation efficiency showed that R2 was higher (0.50) and significant in treatment amended with biochar or both biochar and nutrient/fertiliser (p < 0.01), compared to treatment with nutrient/fertiliser only or no amendment (R2 = 0.11). This suggest that one of the key impacts of biochar is enhancing microbial biomass and thus the biodegradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar represents a promising biostimulation agent for the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. However, there remains key questions to be answered.

Title: Bacteria-white-rot fungi joint remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil based on sustained-release of laccase
Snippet: The development of the petroleum industry has signicantly promoted the growth of the global economy. However, in the exploitation, transportation, and processing of oil, large volumes of petroleum hydrocarbons have contaminated the environment because of oil spillages and accidents. 1 At present, many areas have been subjected to ecological risk from petroleum-contaminated soil. 2,3 2][13][14] In research on the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil, researchers have found many microorganisms which can be used to biodegrade petroleum hydrocarbons. 8][19][20][21][22] With different physiological characteristics, bacteria and white-rot fungi present dissimilar features in the remediation of petroleumcontaminated soil. With their simple structures and small size, bacteria show strong adaptability to environmental change and are easily propagated. However, their capacity to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons with complex structures is poor. ][25][26] Considering the bad environmental conditions like the high oil and salt content, using bacteria and white-rot fungi alone cannot guarantee a good remediation effect. ][29] Therefore, to solve the above problems, this research adopted a new way for white-rot fungi to play a full part in the degradation ability of both bacteria and fungi, with other factors, and designed a new remediation system combining bacteria and white-rot fungi. 

In this system, a fungal remediation material was formed through SSF of white-rot fungi, which had better stability and enzyme production efficiency. By covering the soil surface or inserting fungal remediation material into the soil, this system slowly released degrading enzymes to the soil. Meanwhile, by applying bacteria with a high degradation capacity for petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil, the joint degradation thereof was realised. In the meantime, sand and straw were added to improve the physical, and chemical, properties of the soil. Moreover, biosurfactants were added to increase the solubility of the petroleum hydrocarbon in the soil. Finally, by performing orthogonal experiments, the mutual effects of each component in the remediation of soil were studied.

Title: The Effect of Pyrolysis Temperature of calotropis procera Biochar on Dynamics of Petroleum Hydrocarbons Degradation, Carbon Emission, and Ammonia Volatilization in Artificial Petroleum-Contaminated Soil
Snippet: Global population growth and industrial development have increased the demand for petroleum products, hence increasing environmental pollution risk. All this led to the urgent need for new strategies to remediate this pollution. The importance of this study lies in that it provides a new vision for using biochar to rehabilitate and reclaim petroleum-contaminated soils. Therefore, the goals of the study are to test using calotropis procera biochar produced at pyrolysis temperatures of 400 and 650 °C on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation and quality indicators in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil. Applying calotropis procera biochar to artificial petroleumcontaminated soil increased the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar prepared at 400 °C showed more effectiveness in degrading petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil than biochar prepared at 650 °C. Biochar produced by lowtemperature pyrolysis has played an important role in reducing ammonia volatilization from the soil. Low-temperature biochar effectively ameliorates phosphorus availability in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil than biochar produced by hightemperature. High-temperature biochar increases the electrical conductivity than low-temperature biochar. Our results support the hypotheses of this study that pyrolysis temperatures of biochar have a significant impact on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation, ammonia volatilization, and nutrient availability. Accordingly, biochar prepared at low temperatures is a more suitable strategy for the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil while biochar prepared at high temperatures consumes large amounts of energy and loses some nutrients. The results of the current study contribute to finding sustainable solutions for the rehabilitation of petroleum-contaminated soil through the applications of biochar. Biochar is currently used as a soil amendment because of its several agricultural, economic, and environmental benefits.

However, in the exploitation, transportation, and processing of oil, large volumes of petroleum hydrocarbons have contaminated the environment because of oil spillages and accidents. 1 At present, many areas have been subjected to ecological risk from petroleum-contaminated soil. 2,3 2][13][14] In research on the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil, researchers have found many microorganisms which can be used to biodegrade petroleum hydrocarbons. 8][19][20][21][22] With different physiological characteristics, bacteria and white-rot fungi present dissimilar features in the remediation of petroleumcontaminated soil. With their simple structures and small size, bacteria show strong adaptability to environmental change and are easily propagated. However, their capacity to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons with complex structures is poor. ][25][26] Considering the bad environmental conditions like the high oil and salt content, using bacteria and white-rot fungi alone cannot guarantee a good remediation effect. ][29] Therefore, to solve the above problems, this research adopted a new way for white-rot fungi to play a full part in the degradation ability of both bacteria and fungi, with other factors, and designed a new remediation system combining bacteria and white-rot fungi. 

In this system, a fungal remediation material was formed through SSF of white-rot fungi, which had better stability and enzyme production efficiency. By covering the soil surface or inserting fungal remediation material into the soil, this system slowly released degrading enzymes to the soil. Meanwhile, by applying bacteria with a high degradation capacity for petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil, the joint degradation thereof was realised. In the meantime, sand and straw were added to improve the physical, and chemical, properties of the soil. Moreover, biosurfactants were added to increase the solubility of the petroleum hydrocarbon in the soil. Finally, by performing orthogonal experiments, the mutual effects of each component in the remediation of soil were studied.

documents.title: The Effect of Pyrolysis Temperature of calotropis procera Biochar on Dynamics of Petroleum Hydrocarbons Degradation, Carbon Emission, and Ammonia Volatilization in Artificial Petroleum-Contaminated Soil
documents.snippet: Global population growth and industrial development have increased the demand for petroleum products, hence increasing environmental pollution risk. All this led to the urgent need for new strategies to remediate this pollution. The importance of this study lies in that it provides a new vision for using biochar to rehabilitate and reclaim petroleum-contaminated soils. Therefore, the goals of the study are to test using calotropis procera biochar produced at pyrolysis temperatures of 400 and 650 °C on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation and quality indicators in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil. Applying calotropis procera biochar to artificial petroleumcontaminated soil increased the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons. Biochar prepared at 400 °C showed more effectiveness in degrading petroleum hydrocarbons in the soil than biochar prepared at 650 °C. Biochar produced by lowtemperature pyrolysis has played an important role in reducing ammonia volatilization from the soil. Low-temperature biochar effectively ameliorates phosphorus availability in artificial petroleum-contaminated soil than biochar produced by hightemperature. High-temperature biochar increases the electrical conductivity than low-temperature biochar. Our results support the hypotheses of this study that pyrolysis temperatures of biochar have a significant impact on petroleum hydrocarbons degradation, ammonia volatilization, and nutrient availability. Accordingly, biochar prepared at low temperatures is a more suitable strategy for the remediation of petroleum-contaminated soil while biochar prepared at high temperatures consumes large amounts of energy and loses some nutrients. The results of the current study contribute to finding sustainable solutions for the rehabilitation of petroleum-contaminated soil through the applications of biochar. Biochar is currently used as a soil amendment because of its several agricultural, economic, and environmental benefits.

Title: Advancements in Biochar for Soil Remediation of Heavy Metals and/or Organic Pollutants
Snippet: Petroleum hydrocarbons, including gasoline, kerosene, diesel, lubricants, paraffin, and asphalt, are common organic pollutants in the environment. These substances consist of mixtures of various hydrocarbons, such as n-alkanes, branched alkanes, cycloalkanes, and aromatic compounds, along with trace amounts of other organic compounds, including sulfur compounds, nitrogen-containing compounds, and cycloalkanoic acids [36]. The concentrations of petroleum hydrocarbons are notably higher in areas such as oil extraction and processing sites, fueling stations, petroleum spill sites, and agricultural fields near roads. 

The use of biochar can significantly enhance the degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons by soil microorganisms, thereby promoting soil remediation. Wang et al. [37] used biochar derived from the co-pyrolysis of rice husks and cellulose to remediate petroleumcontaminated soils. The results showed that within a 60-day remediation period, the removal rate in the biochar-treated group exceeded 67%, which was approximately 1.4 times higher than that of the microbial control group, which had a removal rate of 46.69%. Moreover, the abundance of petroleum-degrading bacteria, such as Proteus spp., significantly increased, suggesting that biochar addition substantially enhanced microbial growth and degradation activity. The synergistic interaction between biochar and soil microorganisms contributed to the effective removal of petroleum hydrocarbons. Qin et al. [38] examined the effects of straw-based biochar on bioremediation and the microbial community composition over a 180-day period. Their results indicated that the degradation efficiency of total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs) in biochar-amended soils was notably higher than in unamended soils. The timing of biochar addition also influenced degradation efficiency, with the peak TPH removal rate (84.8%) occurring when biochar was added on day 80. At this point, a substantial amount of petroleum hydrocarbon metabolites were absorbed by the biochar, leading to a significant reduction in soil toxicity and enhanced biodegradation activity.

Title: Effect of the Application of Ochrobactrum sp.-Immobilised Biochar on the Remediation of Diesel-Contaminated Soil
Snippet: Crude oil is an important natural resource for energy generation and the production of raw materials for the industry. The 2% average per annual increase in global oil consumption between 1965 and 2020 attests to how relevant oil remains to the world [1]. Nonetheless, petroleum/crude oil leakage and accidental release into the environment frequently occur during the exploration, refining, transportation, and storage of petroleum/crude oil and its derived products [2]. Soil pollution by petroleum hydrocarbons is a common problem in many countries [3,4]. For example, in Nigeria, between 2006 and June 2022, 4102 crude and refined oil spills on land were reported in the country's oil spill monitor [4]. Diesel is a product of crude oil, a frequent progenitor for petroleum hydrocarbon pollution in the environment [5]. Acute and chronic effects on humans and plants occur after exposure to diesel oil [6]. For example, Bona et al. [7] reported that the seedling growth of Schinus terebinthifolius was significantly affected by exposure to diesel. 

Remediation of crude oil-contaminated soils is necessary due to the detrimental effects of exposure to this contaminant [8]. Although several remediation techniques are available for oil/petroleum hydrocarbon-impacted environments [9], remediation of contaminated soil remains a concern. This is owing to the shortcomings associated with existing remediation techniques. For example, thermal desorption is expensive and prone to secondary pollution [10]. Recently, biochar has gained relevance in the remediation of hydrocarbon-contaminated soil. Biochar is a carbon-based product obtained from the thermochemical decomposition of biomass, including waste materials, in an oxygenlimited environment [11]. The application of biochar to contaminated soil has been shown to enhance hydrocarbon removal by up to 2.1 times [12][13][14]. For example, Aziz, Ali, Farooq, Jamal, Liu, He, Guo, Urynowicz and Huang [12] showed that adding sludgederived biochar led to a minimum of 101% greater removal than the control treatment.

Title: Advancements in Biochar for Soil Remediation of Heavy Metals and/or Organic Pollutants
Snippet: The findings indicated that the Serratia-loaded biochar efficiently degraded total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs) in the soil, achieving a degradation rate of 82.5%. During the remediation process, the activities of soil dehydrogenase (SDHA) and catalase (CAT) increased by 14% and 15-fold, respectively. In addition to the studies mentioned above, Yousaf et al. [43] investigated the combined effect of biochar and plants in the remediation of petroleum hydrocarbons, using leguminous and gramineous plants along with wood-based biochar. The results revealed that compared with biochar alone (with a total petroleum hydrocarbon degradation rate of 27%), the biochar-plant combined remediation approach resulted in a significantly higher reduction in petroleum hydrocarbons (68%). The combined application of biochar with leguminous plants led to a higher removal rate of petroleum hydrocarbons than the use of gramineous plants such as maize, wheat, and ryegrass. 

In summary, biochar, as a sustainable adsorbent material and immobilization carrier, can effectively adsorb petroleum hydrocarbons in soil, preventing the diffusion of pollutants into aquatic and atmospheric environments. By adsorbing petroleum hydrocarbons, biochar also increases the surface area available for microbial interaction with the contaminants, promoting their biodegradation. While biochar alone may exhibit limited effectiveness in remediating petroleum hydrocarbons, the combined biochar-plant remediation approach shows considerable promise. Biochar enhances the growth of beneficial microorganisms in plants, making this combined approach not only environmentally sustainable but also economically viable.

Title: Progress in biostimulation-based remediation of TPH-contaminated soils: a comprehensive review
Snippet: To begin with, biochar possesses a significant ability to adsorb substances and exhibits enhanced stability, which can efficiently decrease the levels of heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons, and various other contaminants (Ali et al., 2019;Mansoor et al., 2021). Biochar primarily enhances the breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by stimulating biological activity. It creates an optimal environment for microorganisms, encouraging the proliferation of native microbial populations, which in turn boosts the rate of TPH degradation (Ren et al., 2022;Kong et al., 2018;Li et al., 2022b). Yu et al. (2019) remediated petroleum hydrocarbon contaminated soils by using biochar and mineral fertilizer, and the comparison of them found that their dominant bacterial flora were different, which proved that biochar could promote the certain microbial growth. Second, biochar can improve the water content of soil, which is favorable for the microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons (Saeed et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2022b;Zhang et al., 2019). In addition, biochar materials have surface functional groups that can supplement specific nutrients to soil microorganisms, thereby promoting their growth (Dike et al., 2021;Zama et al., 2018). Saeed et al. (2021) found that the nitrogen content of biochar-treated soils increased by 23% and 16%, phosphorus content by 10-5%, and potassium content by 5-3%, respectively, under 10% and 15% oil contamination compared to the non-biochar treatment. The role of biochar in restoring petroleum hydrocarbon-contaminated soils is illustrated in Fig. 1, highlighting mechanisms such as sorption, microbial stimulation, and reduction of contaminant mobility. Biochar can act through two distinct mechanisms: sorption and nutrient amendment. Sorption refers to biochar's ability to physically adsorb or chemically bind petroleum hydrocarbons onto its porous surface, reducing their mobility and toxicity.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer completely fails the verification criterion. Instead of rejecting the premise, it affirms it throughout, claiming that 'demonstrated, replicated success' of the five-component combination 'accelerated adoption' and converted it 'into a standardized remediation toolkit.'
